The Duke of Parma recovered the south for Spain in the 1580s but could not force the great rivers, and that line became the border between the modern Netherlands and Belgium.

What emerged in the north was a federation of provinces governed by their merchant regents, with the House of Orange holding military command. It financed the war with a public debt that lenders trusted at low interest, and its trade grew during it: the [East India Company](event:dutch-east-india) was chartered in 1602, in the middle of a war for survival. By 1648 it was the leading commercial power in Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighty_Years%27_War).

steps.name: Alba's tribunal and the first campaigns
steps.page:
The Duke of Alba's Council of Troubles condemned thousands and executed over a thousand, including the counts of Egmont and Hoorn, and his new tenth-penny sales tax united merchants against him.

William of Orange's invasions from Germany in 1568 failed, and the war seemed over before it had begun.

steps.name: The Sea Beggars take Brielle
steps.page:
Expelled from English ports, a fleet of exiled privateers called the Sea Beggars seized the little port of Brielle on 1 April 1572 almost by accident, finding it ungarrisoned.

Town after town in Holland and Zeeland then declared for Orange. The revolt had territory, and a coastline it could hold against an army that had no fleet.

steps.name: The Pacification of Ghent
steps.page:
Unpaid Spanish troops mutinied and sacked Antwerp in November 1576, killing several thousand people in what became known as the Spanish Fury.

Within days almost all seventeen provinces, Catholic and Protestant, signed the Pacification of Ghent demanding the withdrawal of foreign troops. It was the nearest the Low Countries came to holding together.

steps.name: Union of Utrecht and the Act of Abjuration
steps.page:
The unity did not last. Catholic southern provinces formed the Union of Arras in January 1579 and made terms with Spain; northern provinces answered days later with the Union of Utrecht, a defensive league that became the constitution of the Dutch Republic.

In July 1581 the States General passed the Act of Abjuration, declaring that a prince who oppresses his subjects forfeits their obedience, and renouncing Philip II.

steps.name: Parma's reconquest and the fall of Antwerp
steps.page:
The Duke of Parma, the ablest commander of the war, retook the southern cities one by one and closed on Antwerp, then the greatest port in northern Europe. It fell in August 1585 after a fourteen-month siege and a bridge of boats across the Scheldt.

Its Protestant merchants were given four years to leave, and most went north to Amsterdam with their capital and trade connections. The Dutch closed the Scheldt, and Antwerp's commerce never returned. Parma could not force the great rivers, and the line held there.

steps.name: The Twelve Years' Truce
steps.page:
Exhausted and bankrupt, Spain agreed a truce in April 1609 that treated the Republic as a state in all but name. The Dutch used the twelve years to expand their trade in Asia and the Atlantic.

At home the truce let a bitter religious and political quarrel between Remonstrants and Counter-Remonstrants come into the open, ending with the execution of the land's advocate, Oldenbarnevelt, in 1619.

steps.name: The Peace of Münster
steps.page:
War resumed in 1621 and merged into the [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war). Dutch fleets destroyed a Spanish armada in the Downs in 1639 and took Brazilian and Asian territory from the Portuguese.

By the treaty signed at Münster on 15 May 1648, Spain recognised the United Provinces as free and independent, ceded conquests in the south, and accepted the closure of the Scheldt. The Republic entered its golden age.

name: Battle of Lepanto
summary: On 7 October 1571 the fleet of a Catholic Holy League destroyed an Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras off western Greece. It was the largest naval battle of the century and one of the last fought mainly by oared galleys.
body:
Part of [Ottoman wars in Europe](event:ottoman-wars-europe). The league was assembled by Pope Pius V after the Ottoman invasion of Venetian Cyprus, and drew ships from Spain, Venice, Genoa, the Papal States, Savoy and the Knights of Malta. Don John of Austria, half-brother of Philip II, commanded some 210 galleys against about 250 under Ali Pasha.

The Venetians brought six *galleasses*, large converted merchantmen carrying heavy guns on every side, and stationed them ahead of the line; their fire broke the Ottoman formation before the fleets met. After that the fighting was hand to hand across lashed decks. Ali Pasha was killed, most of the Ottoman fleet was captured or sunk, and some 12,000 Christian galley slaves were freed. Miguel de Cervantes, then a soldier, was shot twice in the chest and lost the use of his left hand.

Cyprus was not recovered, and the Ottomans had a new fleet at sea by the next campaigning season; a grand vizier is said to have remarked that Venice had merely singed his beard. It was the last major engagement of the galley age.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lepanto).

name: St Bartholomew's Day massacre
summary: The killing of Huguenot leaders and thousands of Protestants in Paris and the provinces, beginning on 24 August 1572.
body:
Part of [French Wars of Religion](event:french-wars-religion). The Huguenot nobility had gathered in Paris for the marriage of Henry of Navarre to Margaret of Valois, sister of Charles IX, arranged as a reconciliation. An attempt on the life of Admiral Coligny, the Huguenot leader, failed on 22 August.

Two days later the king's council ordered the killing of the leaders, and the Paris militia and crowds extended it to the Huguenot population of the city. The killing spread to Orleans, Lyon, Rouen, Bordeaux and other towns over the following weeks. Estimates of the dead range from about 5,000 to 30,000.

Navarre saved himself by converting. The Huguenot movement lost most of its senior commanders, took a harder political line, and the wars continued for another twenty-six years. Pope Gregory XIII had a commemorative medal struck; Protestant Europe treated the massacre as evidence of what a Catholic settlement would mean.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Bartholomew%27s_Day_massacre).

name: Defeat of the Spanish Armada
summary: Philip II sent a fleet of about 130 ships in 1588 to escort an invasion army from the Netherlands to England. English gunnery, fireships and Atlantic weather broke it up, and roughly half the ships never returned to Spain.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). The expedition answered English raiding of Spanish shipping and treasure, English support for the [Dutch revolt](event:netherlands-independence), and the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, in 1587. The plan required the fleet to reach the Flemish coast and ferry the Duke of Parma's veteran army across the Channel, but Parma's barges could not get out past Dutch shallow-draught blockaders, and there was no deep-water port the Armada could hold while it waited.

The Spanish came up the Channel in July in a crescent formation that the English could not break, fighting running actions at long range with little effect on either side. The Armada anchored off Calais; at midnight eight English fireships were sent in, and the Spanish cut their cables and scattered. The battle of Gravelines the next day did real damage at close range. With the wind against them and their anchors gone, the survivors ran north around Scotland and Ireland, where storms wrecked many ships on the coast.

England's danger was not over. Further armadas sailed in the 1590s, and Spain remained the greater power for another half-century, but the defeat became a founding story of English Protestant identity. The commemorative medal read: *He blew with His winds, and they were scattered*.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Armada).

name: Dutch Golden Age
summary: The period of Dutch commercial, scientific and artistic predominance in the seventeenth century, resting on trade, shipping and the finance of the new republic.
body:
The Dutch Republic emerged from the [revolt against Spain](event:netherlands-independence) as a federation of seven provinces with no monarch, an unusual degree of religious tolerance and the highest urbanisation rate in Europe. Antwerp's fall in 1585 sent much of its merchant community, and its capital, north to Amsterdam.

Trade was the base: the Baltic grain trade, the herring fishery, the fluyt, a cheap bulk carrier with a small crew, and the chartered companies for [Asia](event:dutch-east-india) and the Atlantic. Amsterdam had a public exchange bank from 1609 and a stock exchange trading company shares, forwards and options.

Painting was produced for an open market rather than for church or court, which is why so much of it is landscape, still life, genre and portraiture; Rembrandt, Vermeer, Hals and Ruisdael worked in these decades. Printing was comparatively free of censorship, so Descartes, Spinoza and Locke published there.

The invasion of 1672 by France and England, the rampjaar or disaster year, is the usual end point. The republic survived, but as a second-rank power carrying a heavy debt.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Golden_Age).

name: Shakespeare's plays
summary: William Shakespeare wrote about thirty-eight plays for the London commercial theatre between roughly 1589 and 1613. They are the most performed and most translated body of drama in any language.
body:
[Shakespeare](item:william-shakespeare) wrote for a repertory company he part-owned, the Lord Chamberlain's Men, renamed the King's Men on James I's accession in 1603, which played at the Theatre, then at the Globe from 1599, and at the indoor Blackfriars from 1608. This was commercial work for a mixed audience standing in the yard and seated in the galleries, performed in daylight on a bare stage with almost no scenery, where place is established by the words.

The usual grouping is comedies, histories and tragedies, with the late plays, among them *The Winter's Tale* and *The Tempest*, set apart as romances. Almost every plot is borrowed, from Holinshed's chronicles, from Plutarch, from Italian novellas. What is not borrowed is the language and the interiority: soliloquy is used to show a mind changing while it speaks, in *Hamlet* and *Macbeth* above all.

About half the plays were unpublished when he died in 1616, and survive only because two fellow actors, John Heminges and Henry Condell, collected thirty-six of them in the First Folio of 1623. They have been adapted, cut, rewritten with happy endings and restored again over four centuries, and have been performed continuously since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare%27s_plays).

name: Japanese invasions of Korea
summary: Two Japanese invasions of Korea under Toyotomi Hideyoshi, in 1592 and 1597, opposed by Korean forces and a Ming Chinese army. The Japanese withdrew after Hideyoshi's death in 1598.
body:
Toyotomi Hideyoshi, having completed the [unification of Japan](event:sengoku-unification), demanded passage through Korea for an invasion of Ming China. Korea refused, and about 158,000 men landed at Busan in May 1592.

The invaders took the capital in under three weeks and Pyongyang by July, but could not hold the country. At sea Yi Sun-sin destroyed successive Japanese squadrons and cut the supply route round the peninsula; on land, local militias attacked the garrisons; and a Ming army entered the war and retook Pyongyang in February 1593. The front settled on a line of Japanese fortresses along the south coast.

Negotiations broke down and a second invasion came in 1597. It was held in the south, and Yi Sun-sin, restored to command after being dismissed and imprisoned, destroyed a much larger fleet at [Myeongnyang](event:myeongnyang) with thirteen ships. Hideyoshi died in 1598 and the armies were withdrawn.

The war is known in Korea as the Imjin War, after the year of its outbreak in the sexagenary cycle. Korean losses in population, farmland and cultural property were severe; the Ming treasury was strained; and in Japan the Toyotomi house was weakened.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imjin_War).

steps.name: The landing at Busan
steps.page:
The first Japanese division under Konishi Yukinaga crossed from Tsushima and landed at Busan on 23 May 1592. The garrison fortresses of Busan and Dongnae were taken within two days. In all about 158,000 men were shipped over in the following weeks.

The Korean army had no experience of a war of this size and few firearms, while the Japanese commanders had been fighting continuously for thirty years and were equipped with matchlocks. Three divisions advanced north by separate roads towards the capital.

steps.name: Chungju and the fall of the capital
steps.page:
The Korean field army under Sin Rip met the Japanese at Chungju on 6 June and was destroyed on open ground where its cavalry was shot down. King Seonjo left the capital, which was entered on 10 June, and went north to Uiju on the Yalu to ask for Ming help.

Pyongyang fell on 20 July. Kato Kiyomasa's division reached the Tumen in the far north east. Behind the advance, local militias known as righteous armies attacked garrisons and supply columns, and the country people refused to supply the invaders.

steps.name: Yi Sun-sin at sea
steps.page:
Yi Sun-sin, commander of the left Jeolla naval district, took his squadron east in the summer of 1592 and destroyed Japanese shipping at Okpo, Sacheon and Danghangpo. His ships carried heavier cannon than the Japanese and did not close to be boarded.

On 14 August he drew the main Japanese fleet out of the narrow Gyeonnaeryang strait into open water near Hansan Island and enveloped it, sinking most of it. The Korean navy kept control of the south western sea route, so the armies in the north could not be supplied by sea round the peninsula.

steps.name: The Ming intervention
steps.page:
A Ming army of about 40,000 under Li Rusong crossed the Yalu at the end of 1592 and retook Pyongyang on 8 February 1593 with heavy artillery. The Japanese fell back on the capital.

Li's advance guard was checked at Byeokjegwan north of Hanseong in late February. A Korean force under Gwon Yul then held the fortified hill of Haengju against a much larger attack on 14 March. With supplies short on both sides, the Japanese evacuated the capital in May and withdrew to a line of fortresses on the southern coast.

steps.name: The coastal fortresses and the truce
steps.page:
From the summer of 1593 the Japanese held a chain of fortresses along the south coast from Ulsan to Suncheon while envoys negotiated. The second siege of Jinju in July 1593 was taken and its garrison and townspeople killed.

The talks failed because each side was told what its own negotiators thought it wished to hear: Hideyoshi believed he was being offered a Ming princess and the southern provinces, and the Ming court believed he was accepting investiture as king of Japan. When the misunderstanding became clear in 1596 the war resumed.

steps.name: Noryang and the withdrawal
steps.page:
Hideyoshi died on 18 September 1598 and the council governing for his heir ordered the armies home. The Ming and Korean forces pressed the coastal fortresses through the autumn.

On the night of 16 December the allied fleet attacked the Japanese ships covering the evacuation in the Noryang strait. Most of the Japanese squadron was destroyed. Yi Sun-sin was killed by a musket shot during the pursuit. The last troops left Korea within weeks, and the peninsula was left with its farmland, records and population heavily reduced.

name: Battle of Myeongnyang
summary: Yi Sun-sin defeated a much larger Japanese fleet in the Myeongnyang strait on 26 October 1597 with thirteen ships, stopping the Japanese advance by sea.
body:
Part of [Japanese invasions of Korea](event:imjin-war). Yi Sun-sin had been removed from command and imprisoned in 1597 after refusing an order he believed was based on false intelligence. His successor lost almost the whole Korean fleet at Chilcheollyang in August, and Yi was reinstated with thirteen ships.

He met the Japanese fleet on 26 October in the Myeongnyang strait between the mainland and Jindo, a channel about 300 metres wide where the tidal current runs very fast and reverses. The Japanese ships, reported at over 130, could enter only a few at a time and could not manoeuvre; the Korean ships fought at anchor across the channel and used the turn of the tide.

The Japanese lost about thirty ships and broke off. The advance up the west coast was stopped and the invasion did not recover the initiative at sea.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Myeongnyang).

name: Edict of Nantes
summary: Henry IV of France issued the Edict of Nantes in April 1598, granting Huguenots freedom of conscience, limited freedom of worship and equal civil rights. It ended the French Wars of Religion, which had run for thirty-six years.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). Henry was himself a Huguenot who had converted to Catholicism in 1593 to secure Paris and the throne. The edict allowed Protestant worship where it was already established and in one town per judicial district, but not in Paris; it opened offices and universities to Huguenots and gave them courts of mixed membership to hear their cases. Secret articles granted them some 150 fortified towns, garrisoned at royal expense, which is the part Catholics objected to most.

The military privileges were removed by Louis XIII after the siege of La Rochelle in 1628, though the religious clauses stood. Louis XIV then dismantled those too, first by harassment and forced billeting, and in 1685 revoked the edict outright by the Edict of Fontainebleau, ordering churches pulled down, ministers exiled and Protestant children baptised as Catholics.

Perhaps 200,000 Huguenots left France for England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia, Switzerland and the American colonies, taking skills in weaving, watchmaking, printing and finance with them. The edict was one of the earliest laws in Europe to give a religious minority a legal standing.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Nantes).

name: Time of Troubles
summary: A period of dynastic crisis, famine, civil war and foreign occupation in Russia between 1598 and 1613. It ended with the election of Michael Romanov as tsar.
body:
The Rurikid line ended with the death of Fyodor I in 1598 and the throne passed to Boris Godunov, who was elected by an assembly. A famine from 1601 to 1603, caused by crop failures that followed a volcanic eruption in Peru, is estimated to have killed about two million people, a third of the population.

In 1604 a man claiming to be Dmitry, the youngest son of Ivan IV who had died in 1591, invaded with Polish backing and was crowned in 1605. He was killed within a year, and a second and a third false Dmitry followed. Cossack and peasant risings, boyar factions, Swedish intervention in the north and a Polish army in Moscow from 1610 left the state without a working government.

A volunteer army raised in Nizhny Novgorod by the merchant Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky retook Moscow in the autumn of 1612. An assembly elected the sixteen year old Michael Romanov as tsar in 1613, beginning a dynasty that ruled until 1917. Peace with Sweden followed in 1617 and with Poland in 1618.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_of_Troubles).

name: English East India Company founded
summary: Elizabeth I chartered the East India Company in December 1600 as a joint-stock venture for trade with Asia. Over two centuries it became a territorial power, ruling much of India with its own armies, until the Crown took over in 1858.
body:
The company began with a monopoly of English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope and a handful of ships. Pushed out of the spice islands by the Dutch, a contest settled by the killing of English merchants at Amboyna in 1623, it concentrated on India, trading silver and bullion for cotton textiles, indigo, saltpetre and later tea, from factories at Surat, Madras, Bombay and Calcutta held by permission of Indian rulers and defended by small garrisons.

Its transformation came in Bengal. Victory at [Plassey](event:battle-plassey) in 1757 made the company the power behind the nawab, and in 1765 it obtained the *diwani*, the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. From then it taxed and governed as well as traded, and paid for its Indian armies out of Indian revenue. The Bengal famine of 1770, in which perhaps a third of the province died, followed within five years.

Parliament regulated it in stages, through the Regulating Act of 1773, Pitt's India Act of 1784 and the impeachment of Warren Hastings, and stripped its trade monopolies in 1813 and 1833, leaving it an administration with a private army of over 200,000 men. After the rebellion of 1857 it was wound up and India passed directly to the Crown.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company).

name: Battle of Sekigahara
summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated the coalition led by Ishida Mitsunari on 21 October 1600, which led to his appointment as shogun and to 250 years of Tokugawa rule.
body:
Part of [Unification of Japan](event:sengoku-unification). After Toyotomi Hideyoshi died in 1598 leaving a five year old heir, the regents fell out. Tokugawa Ieyasu, the strongest of them, was opposed by a coalition assembled by Ishida Mitsunari in the name of the Toyotomi house.

The armies, each of about 80,000 men, met in fog in the valley at Sekigahara on the road between the capital and the east on 21 October 1600. The fighting was even until Kobayakawa Hideaki, posted on the hill of Matsuo with 15,000 men, changed sides and attacked the western flank. Other contingents followed and the coalition collapsed. Ishida was captured and executed.

Ieyasu redistributed the domains of the defeated, took the title of shogun in 1603 and moved the seat of government to Edo. The distinction between the fudai daimyo who had supported him and the tozama who had not was built into the structure of [Tokugawa Japan](event:edo-japan).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sekigahara).

name: Dutch East India Company founded
summary: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was chartered in 1602 with a monopoly of Dutch trade in Asia and the power to make war, sign treaties and plant colonies on its own account. It is usually described as the first company with permanent, publicly traded shares.
body:
The charter merged competing Dutch ventures into one and granted twenty-one years of monopoly, renewed repeatedly thereafter. Its shares traded on the Amsterdam exchange, which developed forward contracts, short selling and the rest of the machinery of a securities market around them. Capital was permanent rather than repaid after each voyage, which is what allowed the company to build forts, fleets and a standing administration.

It pursued monopoly by force. Jan Pieterszoon Coen founded Batavia on the ruins of Jayakarta in 1619, and in 1621 destroyed the population of the Banda Islands, who were killed, starved or deported, to take the nutmeg trade, repopulating the islands with enslaved labour under Dutch planters. The company took Malacca from Portugal in 1641, held the Cape from 1652, and from 1641 had the only European access to Japan, at Dejima in Nagasaki harbour.

At its height it employed tens of thousands, sent about a million Europeans east, and paid steady dividends for most of two centuries. War with Britain, corruption among its servants and the cost of governing territory in Java eroded it, and it was dissolved in 1799, its debts and possessions passing to the Dutch state.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company).

name: Tokugawa Japan and sakoku
summary: The Tokugawa shoguns ruled Japan from Edo, now Tokyo, from 1603 to 1868. They kept internal peace for two and a half centuries and, from the 1630s, restricted foreign contact almost to nothing, the policy later called *sakoku*, the closed country.
body:
Tokugawa Ieyasu won at Sekigahara in 1600 and took the title of shogun in 1603. The regime controlled some 260 daimyo domains through hostage-taking and expense: *sankin-kotai* required each lord to spend alternate years at Edo and to leave his family there permanently, and the processions and double households consumed the wealth that might have paid for rebellion. Society was ordered in fixed status groups; the emperor remained at Kyoto without power.

Christianity was suppressed after the Shimabara rebellion of 1637–38, Japanese were forbidden to leave or return, and foreign trade was confined to a Dutch post on the artificial island of Dejima together with Chinese, Korean and Ryukyuan channels. Foreign contact was licensed rather than ended. Peace brought a long expansion of cities, roads, commerce and literacy, of kabuki and woodblock printing, and of *rangaku*, Dutch learning, through which European anatomy and astronomy reached Japanese scholars.

By the nineteenth century the samurai were indebted, the currency was debased and famine had provoked risings. Commodore Perry's American squadron forced the ports open in 1853–54, unequal treaties followed, and the discredited shogunate fell to domains from the south-west in the [Meiji Restoration](event:meiji) of 1868.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edo_period).

name: Jamestown settlement
summary: Jamestown, founded in May 1607 on a river in Virginia, was the first permanent English settlement in North America. It nearly failed several times before tobacco made it viable, and it became the capital of the colony of Virginia.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). The Virginia Company sent about a hundred men and boys to look for gold and a passage to the Pacific. The site they chose was defensible and malarial, with brackish water. Most of the first arrivals were dead within a year of disease, hunger and fighting, and in the starving time of the winter of 1609–10 the population fell from several hundred to about sixty; the survivors were boarding ship to abandon the place when a relief fleet arrived.

John Rolfe's planting of a West Indian tobacco variety from 1612 gave Virginia an export. Tobacco is labour-intensive and exhausts soil, so the colony spread along the rivers and needed workers: indentured servants at first, and from 1619, when an English privateer sold some twenty captive Africans at Point Comfort, enslaved Africans in slowly growing numbers. The first representative assembly in English America met at Jamestown the same year.

The Powhatan confederacy, the region's dominant power, attacked in 1622 and again in 1644, killing hundreds of colonists; both were answered with wars of destruction that broke Powhatan power. The capital moved to Williamsburg in 1699 after the statehouse burned, and Jamestown was abandoned to farmland.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamestown,_Virginia).

name: Founding of Quebec
summary: Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec on the St Lawrence in July 1608 as a fur-trading post. It became the capital of New France and the centre of French settlement in North America.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Champlain chose a narrowing of the river below a cliff, *kébec* in Algonquian meaning where the water narrows, which could be defended and could control traffic upstream. Twenty of the first twenty-eight men died of scurvy in the first winter.

The colony lived on beaver pelts, and pelts depended on Indigenous hunters and middlemen, so the French built alliances rather than plantations: with the Innu, the Algonquin and above all the Huron-Wendat. Champlain joined a war party against the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) in 1609, which set the alignment of the next century's conflicts. *Coureurs de bois* travelled and traded deep into the interior, Jesuit missionaries followed them, and the resulting intermarriage produced the Métis peoples of the west.

New France grew slowly, to around 70,000 settlers by the 1750s against well over a million in the British colonies, because the fur trade needed few people and the church discouraged Protestant emigration. Britain took Quebec in 1759 at the battle of the Plains of Abraham during the [Seven Years' War](event:seven-years-war) and kept it in 1763, but the Quebec Act of 1774 preserved French civil law, the language and the Catholic church, and Quebec remains the heart of Francophone North America.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_City#Colonial_era).

name: Kepler's laws of planetary motion
summary: Johannes Kepler published three laws describing how planets move: on ellipses with the Sun at one focus, sweeping equal areas in equal times, with orbital period fixed by distance from the Sun. They replaced two thousand years of circles.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Kepler worked from the observations of Tycho Brahe, the most accurate made before the telescope, which he inherited when Tycho died in 1601. Fitting Mars to a circular orbit left a residual error of eight minutes of arc, a discrepancy earlier astronomers would have set aside and which Kepler took as decisive. The ellipse and the equal-area law appeared in *Astronomia nova* in 1609; the third law, that the square of a planet's period is proportional to the cube of its mean distance, in *Harmonices mundi* in 1619.

He worked on much else. He explained how the eye forms an image on the retina, designed an improved telescope with two convex lenses, wrote on the packing of spheres and on snowflakes, and calculated the *Rudolphine Tables*, far more accurate than anything before them. He believed to the end in a cosmos built on geometric and musical harmony, and he spent a year defending his mother at her trial for witchcraft.

The laws were empirical: they described how the planets move without saying why. [Newton](event:newton) derived all three from the inverse-square law of gravitation in 1687, which is how Kepler's work became part of physics.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_motion).

name: Galileo turns a telescope on the sky
summary: In 1610 Galileo Galilei turned a telescope of his own making on the sky and published what he saw: mountains on the Moon, four moons circling Jupiter, and stars beyond counting in the Milky Way. The phases of Venus followed. The heavens were neither perfect nor centred on the Earth.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Galileo did not invent the telescope but ground better lenses and reached about twenty times magnification. *Sidereus Nuncius*, published in March 1610, made him famous across Europe within months. The moons of Jupiter mattered most: here was plainly a centre of motion that was not the Earth. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, cannot occur at all in the Ptolemaic arrangement.

He worked on mechanics as well. Bodies of different weight fall alike; a body in motion stays in motion unless something stops it; a projectile follows a parabola compounded of uniform and accelerated motion. The demonstration that mathematics describes terrestrial motion is what [Newton](event:newton) built on.

His advocacy of [Copernicus](event:copernicus) brought a warning from the Inquisition in 1616. When his *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* appeared in 1632, with the pope's own argument given to a character named Simplicio, he was tried, made to abjure kneeling, and confined to his villa near Florence for the last nine years of his life. He was blind by 1638 and finished his best book on mechanics, the *Two New Sciences*, under house arrest; it was smuggled out and printed in the Netherlands.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_Galilei).

name: Siege of Osaka
summary: Two campaigns in 1614 and 1615 in which Tokugawa forces destroyed Osaka castle and the Toyotomi house, ending the wars of the Sengoku period.
body:
Part of [Unification of Japan](event:sengoku-unification). Toyotomi Hideyori held Osaka castle, the strongest fortress in Japan, with a garrison swollen by masterless samurai. Tokugawa Ieyasu used an inscription on a temple bell, which could be read as a pun against his name, as the occasion for war.

The winter campaign of 1614 failed against the walls and ended in a truce whose terms allowed the Tokugawa to fill in the outer moats. When fighting resumed in the summer of 1615 the castle had lost its outworks. The defenders were beaten in the open at Tennoji on 3 June and the castle was stormed the next day. Hideyori and his mother died in the ruins.

With the Toyotomi gone the Tokugawa issued the laws governing the military houses and the imperial court, and the country had no large-scale warfare for two centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Osaka).

name: Thirty Years' War
summary: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618 with a revolt in Bohemia and drew in most of Europe before ending at the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. It was fought largely inside the Holy Roman Empire, where armies living off the land brought famine and epidemic; parts of Germany lost a third or more of their people.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). It began as a constitutional and religious quarrel within the empire: the Bohemian estates rejected the Catholic Habsburg Ferdinand as their king and elected the Calvinist Frederick of the Palatinate instead. It became a European war because the Habsburgs of Vienna and Madrid were allies, and because Denmark, Sweden and finally France each intervened rather than let the emperor consolidate power in Germany. France, though Catholic, subsidised the Protestant side for years before joining it openly in 1635.

The armies were large, mercenary and irregularly paid, and were supplied by *contribution*, money and food extracted from whatever territory they stood on, friendly or not. That, with the typhus, plague and dysentery that travelled with them, did most of the killing; the sack of Magdeburg in 1631, in which some 20,000 died, became the war's byword. Wallenstein raised armies as a business venture and was murdered on the emperor's orders when he grew too independent to control.

The settlement of 1648 confirmed the [Peace of Augsburg](event:peace-augsburg), added Calvinism to the recognised confessions, and left the imperial princes with effective sovereignty. Spain recognised Dutch independence; France gained in Alsace and Sweden on the Baltic coast. The empire continued as a legal framework rather than a state, and later writers made 1648 the founding date of a European order of sovereign powers.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War).

steps.name: The Bohemian revolt
steps.page:
Protestant nobles threw two imperial governors and a secretary out of a window of Prague Castle on 23 May 1618, the Defenestration of Prague; all three survived the fall. The estates then deposed the Habsburg Ferdinand and elected Frederick V of the Palatinate king of Bohemia.

Ferdinand, now also emperor, borrowed a Catholic League army under Tilly and Spanish help. Frederick's forces were destroyed at the White Mountain outside Prague on 8 November 1620, and twenty-seven leaders of the revolt were executed in the old town square.

steps.name: The Palatinate campaign
steps.page:
Spanish troops from the Netherlands and imperial armies overran Frederick's own lands on the Rhine while he was losing Bohemia, and Tilly beat his remaining supporters at Wimpfen and Höchst in 1622 and Stadtlohn in 1623.

Frederick's electoral title was transferred to Maximilian of Bavaria, upsetting the confessional balance of the electoral college and giving every Protestant prince a reason to fear the next imperial decision.

steps.name: Danish intervention
steps.page:
Christian IV of Denmark, who was also a duke of the empire and wanted the north German bishoprics for his family, entered the war in 1625 with English and Dutch subsidies.

He was beaten by Tilly at Lutter in 1626 while Wallenstein's new army overran Jutland, and made peace at Lübeck in 1629 on terms that cost him nothing but influence. Emboldened, Ferdinand issued the Edict of Restitution, ordering the return of all church land secularised since 1552, the demand that made a compromise peace impossible.

steps.name: Gustavus Adolphus and the Swedish intervention
steps.page:
Gustavus Adolphus landed in Pomerania in July 1630, financed by France, with an army trained in mobile artillery and combined infantry and cavalry volleys. The sack of Magdeburg in May 1631 by imperial forces, in which some 20,000 died, drove the wavering Protestant electors into his camp.

He destroyed Tilly's army at Breitenfeld in September 1631 and swept to the Rhine and into Bavaria. He was killed leading a cavalry charge in fog at Lützen on 16 November 1632, in a battle his army won.

steps.name: Nördlingen and the Peace of Prague
steps.page:
A Spanish-imperial army crushed the Swedes and their German allies at Nördlingen in September 1634, ending Swedish dominance in the south.

The Peace of Prague in May 1635 suspended the Edict of Restitution, reconciled Saxony and most Lutheran princes with the emperor, and might have ended the war as a German conflict. France declared war on Spain within days.

steps.name: French intervention
steps.page:
Richelieu had subsidised the emperor's enemies for a decade; from 1635 France fought openly, allied with Sweden and the Dutch, and the war lost most of its religious character.

Thirteen more years of campaigning followed across Germany, the Rhineland, the Spanish Netherlands and northern Italy, fought by armies that lived off the countryside. Condé's victory at Rocroi in 1643 broke the reputation of the Spanish infantry, and negotiations opened in Westphalia the same year while the fighting went on.

name: Plymouth Colony
summary: An English colony founded in 1620 in what is now Massachusetts by passengers of the Mayflower, about half of them Separatists from the Church of England.
body:
The Mayflower left Plymouth in September 1620 with 102 passengers, among them a congregation of Separatists who had been living in Leiden. Blown north of the land granted to them, they anchored off Cape Cod in November and, having no legal authority there, drew up the Mayflower Compact, an agreement to govern themselves by majority consent.

They landed at Plymouth in December. About half died during the first winter of scurvy, exposure and disease. The site had been the village of Patuxet, whose inhabitants had been killed by an epidemic between 1616 and 1619; Tisquantum, a survivor who had been taken to Europe as a captive and had returned, acted as interpreter. A treaty was made with the Wampanoag leader Massasoit in 1621 and held for over fifty years.

The harvest feast of 1621 is the usual origin given for the American Thanksgiving. The colony remained small and was absorbed into Massachusetts Bay in 1691. Relations with the Wampanoag ended in the war of 1675 to 1678.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_Colony).

name: Harvey discovers blood circulation
summary: William Harvey showed in 1628 that blood circulates: it is driven by the heart out through the arteries and returns through the veins, in a closed loop. The demonstration overturned the account of the body taught since Galen.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Galen had held that blood is manufactured continuously in the liver from food, moves outward through the veins and is consumed by the tissues, and that some seeps through invisible pores in the wall between the ventricles. Harvey's decisive argument was quantitative: he measured the capacity of the heart, multiplied by the pulse rate, and found that it moves more than the body's own weight of blood in an hour. No liver could make that. The same blood must be coming back.

He supported it with dissection, with vivisection of cold-blooded animals whose hearts beat slowly enough to watch, and with a demonstration anyone could repeat: a ligature on the arm makes the veins stand out, and their valves can be shown to admit blood only towards the heart. *Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis et sanguinis in animalibus* was printed at Frankfurt in 1628, when Harvey was fifty and physician to Charles I.

One link was missing: he could not see how blood crossed from arteries to veins and had to infer it. Marcello Malpighi found the capillaries with a microscope in 1661, four years after Harvey's death. The book is a founding text of experimental physiology.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Harvey).

name: Taj Mahal built
summary: The Taj Mahal is a marble mausoleum at Agra, built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631. Work began in 1632 and the complex was finished about 1653.
body:
Part of [Mughal Empire](event:mughal-empire). The tomb stands on a terrace above the Yamuna, faced in white marble quarried at Makrana and inlaid with jasper, jade, turquoise and lapis in floral patterns, a technique called *pietra dura*, worked by craftsmen from as far as Italy and Persia. The Quranic inscriptions in black marble are cut with letters enlarged as they rise, so that they appear even in height from the ground. The four minarets lean very slightly outward, which would carry them away from the tomb if they fell. A mosque and a matching guest hall in red sandstone flank it, and a *charbagh* garden divided by water channels lies in front.

The chief architect is usually given as Ustad Ahmad Lahauri. Contemporary accounts speak of some 20,000 workers and of materials brought by a thousand elephants. The whole is laid out symmetrically, an order broken only by Shah Jahan's own cenotaph, placed beside his wife's after his death.

Shah Jahan was deposed by his son [Aurangzeb](event:aurangzeb-reign) in 1658 and spent his last years confined in Agra Fort within sight of it. The building was neglected and looted in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, restored under Curzon around 1900, and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site visited by millions a year.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal).

name: Tulip mania
summary: A rise and collapse in the contract prices of tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic in the winter of 1636 to 1637, often cited as the first recorded speculative bubble.
body:
Tulips reached the Netherlands from the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century and became a luxury good, with the most valued varieties carrying flame patterns that are now known to be caused by a virus. Because bulbs can be lifted only in summer, trade in the winter was in contracts for future delivery, settled in taverns and not enforceable in the ordinary courts.

Prices in these contracts rose sharply from the autumn of 1636 and collapsed at auctions in Haarlem in the first days of February 1637. Buyers refused to pay, and in 1638 a formula was adopted allowing contracts to be voided for a few per cent of their face value.

The episode was described as a general madness by contemporary moralising pamphlets and by Charles Mackay in 1841, which is how it entered popular usage. Modern research, in particular by Anne Goldgar, finds that the trade involved a fairly small group of merchants and craftsmen, that few fortunes were destroyed and that the effect on the Dutch economy was slight.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania).

name: English Civil War
summary: Parliament and Charles I fought three civil wars in England, Scotland and Ireland between 1642 and 1651. Parliament won; the king was tried and beheaded in 1649, and the three kingdoms were governed as a republic until the monarchy was restored in 1660.
body:
The quarrel was over money, religion and the limits of royal power at once. Charles ruled for eleven years without calling Parliament, raising revenue by expedients such as ship money, and was forced to recall it in 1640 only when a war he had provoked with Scotland over prayer-book reform went badly. Parliament's demands escalated; a rebellion in Ireland in 1641 raised the question of who should command the army sent to suppress it; and the king raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642.

Parliament's advantages were London, the navy, the customs and the wealth of the south-east. Its instrument was the New Model Army, formed in 1645: professional, regularly paid, promoted on merit and full of religious radicals, with Oliver Cromwell rising through its cavalry. The king was beaten at Marston Moor and Naseby, then made a deal with the Scots that produced a second war in 1648, after which the army purged Parliament, tried him for treason and executed him on 30 January 1649. He was the first European monarch put to death by judicial sentence of his own subjects.

The Commonwealth that followed conquered Ireland and Scotland and settled into Cromwell's Protectorate. It did not outlive him: his son resigned, the army split, and Charles II was restored in 1660. The constitutional questions were reopened in 1688 and settled then.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War).

steps.name: The first war opens
steps.page:
Charles I raised his standard at Nottingham on 22 August 1642 after Parliament had claimed control of the militia. The country divided by region and by interest rather than cleanly: London, the ports and the cloth towns mostly for Parliament, the north and west mostly for the king.

The first pitched battle, at Edgehill on 23 October, was indecisive, and the king's advance on London was turned back at Turnham Green the following month.

steps.name: Marston Moor
steps.page:
Parliament bought Scottish intervention with the Solemn League and Covenant, promising a Presbyterian settlement. The combined armies met Prince Rupert outside York on 2 July 1644 in the largest battle ever fought on English soil.

Cromwell's cavalry broke the royalist right and then turned on the rest. The king lost the north of England in an evening, and Cromwell's reputation was made.

steps.name: The New Model Army and Naseby
steps.page:
Parliament reorganised its forces in February 1645 into a single national army, paid regularly from a national assessment, promoted on merit, and separated from Parliament by the Self-Denying Ordinance.

It destroyed the king's main field army at Naseby on 14 June. His private correspondence was captured with the baggage and published, showing that he had been seeking Irish and Continental troops. The first war ended with his surrender to the Scots in 1646.

steps.name: The second civil war
steps.page:
From captivity Charles negotiated with everyone at once and in December 1647 made an Engagement with the Scots, who invaded on his behalf. Royalist risings broke out in Kent, Essex and South Wales in the spring of 1648.

Cromwell scattered the Scottish army at Preston in August. The army now regarded the king as a man of blood who had renewed a war he had lost, and it would no longer treat with him.

steps.name: The trial and execution of Charles I
steps.page:
Colonel Pride excluded the members who still wanted a settlement with the king, and the remaining Rump established a High Court of Justice. Charles refused to plead, denying that any court could try its sovereign.

He was beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649, wearing two shirts against the cold so that he would not be seen to shiver. The monarchy and the House of Lords were abolished, and England was declared a commonwealth.

steps.name: The conquest of Ireland
steps.page:
Cromwell landed near Dublin in August 1649 to reconquer Ireland, where a Catholic confederacy had allied with royalists. The garrisons of Drogheda and Wexford were put to the sword, and the storming of Drogheda in particular was publicised as a warning to others.

The war and the famine and plague that came with it killed a very large share of the Irish population, and the settlement that followed transferred most Catholic-owned land to Protestant creditors and soldiers.

steps.name: Dunbar and Worcester
steps.page:
The Scots proclaimed Charles II king and took him on Presbyterian terms. Cromwell invaded, was cornered at Dunbar in September 1650 and destroyed a much larger Scottish army there in a dawn attack.

Charles marched south with a new army the following summer and was beaten at Worcester on 3 September 1651, exactly a year later. He escaped abroad after six weeks in hiding. The wars were over, and the three kingdoms were ruled from London until 1660.

name: Isaac Newton
summary: English mathematician and physicist who set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, and who invented the calculus independently of Leibniz.
body:
Newton was born at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire on Christmas Day 1642 by the calendar then used in England, which is 4 January 1643 by the one used now. He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, and did much of his most original work in 1665–67, when plague closed the university and he returned home.

The *[Principia](item:newton)* of 1687 gave three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation, and showed that the same mathematics governs a falling apple, the tides, comets and the orbits of the planets. It is the central text of the [Scientific Revolution](item:scientific-revolution). To carry out the work he developed what he called fluxions, the [calculus](item:calculus), which Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz reached independently and published first, provoking a long priority dispute.

He also wrote the *Opticks*, demonstrated that white light is a mixture of colours, built the first reflecting telescope, spent decades on alchemy and biblical chronology, sat in Parliament, and ran the Royal Mint, where he prosecuted counterfeiters. He was President of the Royal Society from 1703 until his death.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton).

name: Qing dynasty
summary: The Qing were a Manchu dynasty that conquered Ming China from 1644 and ruled until 1912, the last of the imperial dynasties. Under them the empire reached its greatest size, taking in Mongolia, Xinjiang, Tibet and Taiwan, and its population grew from perhaps 150 million to over 400 million.
body:
The Manchus were a confederation from the north-east who entered Beijing in 1644 amid a peasant rebellion that had already destroyed the Ming; resistance in the south lasted four decades. They ruled as a conquest elite: Manchu and Han were kept legally distinct, banner garrisons held the cities, Han men were required to shave the forehead and wear the queue on pain of death, and Manchu shared official business with Chinese. But the Confucian examination bureaucracy was kept intact, which is why the state functioned.

The long reigns of [Kangxi](event:kangxi-emperor), [Yongzheng](event:yongzheng-reforms) and Qianlong covered most of the eighteenth century, a period of peace, territorial expansion and rapid population growth, helped by New World crops such as maize and sweet potato that grew on land rice could not use. Vast scholarly compilations were sponsored, and literary inquisitions ran alongside them.

Pressure came from several directions at once in the nineteenth century: rural poverty and land hunger, a silver drain and the [Opium Wars](event:opium-wars), which opened the treaty ports and exposed the gap in military technology, and then the [Taiping Rebellion](event:taiping), which may have killed twenty million people. Reform came late and partially. The dynasty was overthrown by the revolution of 1911, and the last emperor abdicated in February 1912.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty).

name: Peace of Westphalia
summary: The Peace of Westphalia was concluded in October 1648 by two treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück. It ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire and, in a separate treaty, the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic.
body:
Part of [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war). The negotiations lasted about five years and are usually counted the first modern peace congress: delegations from most of Europe, meeting simultaneously in two Westphalian towns because Catholic and Protestant parties would not sit together, working through mediators and agreed protocols.

The terms were specific rather than philosophical. The [Peace of Augsburg](event:peace-augsburg) was restored and extended to Calvinists, and the religious position of 1624 was made the benchmark for who held what. Imperial princes gained the right to conduct their own foreign policy short of alliances against the emperor. France took Habsburg rights in Alsace and Sweden took territory on the Baltic coast, both with seats in the imperial diet. Spain recognised the independence of the Dutch Republic, and the separation of the Swiss cantons from the empire was confirmed.

Later writers made Westphalia the origin of a system of sovereign states that recognise no superior and do not interfere in one another's internal affairs, called "Westphalian sovereignty". Historians have pointed out that the treaties say nothing so general, and that the empire went on as a legal order above its princes for another century and a half. The term remains in common use.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Westphalia).

name: Khmelnytsky Uprising
summary: A Cossack and peasant rising in Ukraine against Polish-Lithuanian rule, begun in 1648 by Bohdan Khmelnytsky. It led to the Cossack Hetmanate and, by the treaty of Pereiaslav in 1654, to Russian overlordship.
body:
The uprising began in the Zaporozhian Sich in January 1648 under Bohdan Khmelnytsky, a Cossack officer with a private grievance against a Polish neighbour, and grew into a general revolt against the magnates' estates, the Catholic and Uniate churches and the position of the registered Cossacks.

Allied with the Crimean Tatars, Khmelnytsky destroyed Commonwealth armies at Zhovti Vody and Korsun in 1648 and won at Zboriv in 1649. The revolt was accompanied by massacres of Jewish communities in Ukraine, whose scale is debated but which are among the heaviest losses suffered by Jews in Europe before the twentieth century. Polish forces in turn destroyed rebel towns.

After the defeat at Berestechko in 1651 Khmelnytsky sought an outside protector. At Pereiaslav in January 1654 the Cossack council swore allegiance to the tsar, which brought Russia into a thirteen year war with the Commonwealth and, with the Swedish invasion of 1655, opened the period known as [the Deluge](event:deluge).

The truce of Andrusovo in 1667 divided Ukraine along the Dnieper between Russia and the Commonwealth.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmelnytsky_Uprising).

name: The Deluge
summary: The Swedish invasion of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth between 1655 and 1660, fought alongside wars with Russia, Brandenburg and Transylvania. Population losses across the Commonwealth were very heavy.
body:
The Deluge is the Polish name for the wars of 1655 to 1660, in which Swedish armies occupied most of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. It followed the [Khmelnytsky uprising](event:khmelnytsky-uprising) of 1648 and the Russian invasion of 1654, which had already taken Smolensk and much of Lithuania.

Charles X Gustav of Sweden invaded in July 1655 with two armies. Resistance collapsed at first: Greater Poland capitulated at Ujscie, Warsaw and Krakow were taken, and the Lithuanian hetman Janusz Radziwill placed the grand duchy under Swedish protection. John II Casimir left the country.

The occupation then failed. Requisitions and the treatment of churches turned the nobility and the peasantry against the Swedes, the defence of the monastery at Jasna Gora in the winter of 1655 became a rallying point, and a confederation formed at Tyszowce recalled the king. Denmark, Austria and the Dutch republic entered against Sweden and the war ended at Oliva in 1660 with the pre-war borders restored.

Estimates of population loss in the Commonwealth in 1648 to 1660 run from 30 to 50 per cent, with the towns worst affected. The state recovered its territory and not its strength.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deluge_(history)).

steps.name: The Swedish invasion
steps.page:
Two Swedish armies crossed into the Commonwealth in July 1655, one from Swedish Pomerania under Arvid Wittenberg and one from Livonia under Magnus de la Gardie. The Commonwealth was already at war with Russia and had lost Smolensk and much of Lithuania the year before.

The levy of Greater Poland met Wittenberg at Ujscie on 25 July and capitulated the same day; the provincial governors accepted Charles X Gustav as their ruler. Poznan was occupied on 31 July.

steps.name: Warsaw, Krakow and Kiejdany
steps.page:
The Swedish armies advanced without much resistance. Warsaw was entered on 8 September 1655, the first time a foreign army had taken the Polish capital, and Krakow surrendered on 13 October after a siege. John II Casimir left for Silesia.

In Lithuania the hetman Janusz Radziwill signed the union of Kiejdany on 20 October, putting the grand duchy under Swedish protection. Much of the nobility and many towns changed allegiance, though the Swedish demands for money and quarter soon turned opinion.

steps.name: Jasna Gora
steps.page:
A Swedish detachment invested the monastery of Jasna Gora at Czestochowa on 18 November 1655. The house held a much venerated icon and had modern bastioned defences; its prior, Augustyn Kordecki, refused to admit a garrison.

The siege was lifted on 27 December. It was small in military terms, a few thousand besiegers against a few hundred defenders, and large in effect: it was reported across the country as a sign and it coincided with the point at which the szlachta began to change sides.

layers.label: Jasna Gora held, 18 November to 27 December 1655

steps.name: The confederation and the guerrilla war
steps.page:
The confederation formed at Tyszowce on 29 December 1655 declared for John II Casimir, who re-entered the country in January 1656. Peasant bands and irregular cavalry attacked Swedish detachments and convoys, and the occupying army, spread across a large country, could not hold what it had taken.

Stefan Czarniecki's troops beat a Swedish force at Warka on 7 April 1656 and Warsaw was recovered in June. Charles X Gustav's response was to bring in Brandenburg as an ally by the treaty of Konigsberg in January and of Marienburg in June.

steps.name: The three day battle of Warsaw
steps.page:
A Swedish and Brandenburg army of about 18,000 met a Commonwealth force of some 40,000, much of it cavalry and the general levy, north of Warsaw on 28, 29 and 30 July 1656.

The allies held their ground and retook the city, but could not follow the victory up. Russia had declared war on Sweden in July and invaded Livonia, and the Commonwealth's forces remained in the field. The war after 1656 became a matter of sieges, marches and shifting alliances rather than of decisive battles.

steps.name: Oliva
steps.page:
Brandenburg changed sides in 1657 in exchange for sovereignty in Ducal Prussia, and Denmark, Austria and the Dutch republic entered against Sweden. Charles X Gustav turned on Denmark, marched across the frozen Belts, and died in February 1660.

The treaty of Oliva, signed near Danzig on 3 May 1660, restored the pre-war borders in the Commonwealth and had John II Casimir renounce his claim to the Swedish throne. The war with Russia went on to the truce of Andrusovo in 1667, which gave Russia Smolensk and left bank Ukraine.

name: Aurangzeb expands the Mughal Empire
summary: Aurangzeb ruled the Mughal Empire from 1658 to 1707 and extended it over almost the whole Indian subcontinent. The wars that did it drained the treasury, and his enforcement of Islamic orthodoxy alienated Hindu and Sikh subjects; the empire broke apart soon after his death.
body:
Part of [Mughal Empire](event:mughal-empire). He took the throne by defeating his brothers in a war of succession and imprisoning his father Shah Jahan in Agra Fort. He lived austerely by the standards of his dynasty, copied Qurans and sewed caps to earn his own keep, and cared little for the painting and music his predecessors had patronised.

He reversed much of [Akbar](event:akbar-great)'s accommodation. The *jizya* on non-Muslims was reimposed in 1679, a number of temples were destroyed, court music was curtailed, and the ninth Sikh guru, Tegh Bahadur, was executed in 1675, after which the Sikh community turned towards armed organisation. He faced a Rajput revolt, a long Sikh war, and the Marathas under Shivaji, whose mobile raiding he could never bring to a decision.

From 1681 he moved his court permanently to the Deccan and spent twenty-six years there, annexing Bijapur and Golconda but never ending Maratha resistance. The empire reached its greatest extent and its greatest fiscal strain in the same years: the *mansabdari* system had more claimants than assignable revenue, and an army in the field for a generation ate the surplus that paid for it. Within decades of his death in 1707 the provinces were effectively independent, and the [East India Company](event:english-east-india) began dealing with them one at a time.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb).

name: Kangxi Emperor consolidates Qing Dynasty
summary: The Kangxi Emperor reigned from 1661 to 1722, one of the longest reigns in Chinese history. He crushed the revolt that threatened Qing rule in the south, annexed Taiwan, checked Russian expansion and campaigned in Mongolia, leaving a consolidated and prosperous empire.
body:
Part of [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). He came to the throne at seven under regents and took power himself at fifteen. The Revolt of the Three Feudatories, a rising of the Han generals who had helped the Manchus conquer the south, took eight years to put down, from 1673 to 1681, and nearly undid the dynasty. Taiwan, the last Ming loyalist base, was taken in 1683. The Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia in 1689, negotiated in Latin through Jesuit intermediaries, fixed the Amur frontier and was the first treaty China concluded with a European power on equal terms. Campaigns against the Dzungars carried Qing power deep into Mongolia.

He cut taxes repeatedly and in 1712 froze the head-tax quota permanently, repaired the Yellow River works, toured the south six times, and sponsored the Kangxi Dictionary and vast compilations of literature and cartography. He employed Jesuits as astronomers and mathematicians and studied Euclid with them, but ended toleration of Christian missions when Rome forbade Chinese converts to honour their ancestors.

His last years were spoiled by the struggle among his many sons over the succession, which he twice tried and failed to settle. [Yongzheng](event:yongzheng-reforms) succeeded him in 1722 in circumstances still argued over.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangxi_Emperor).

name: Boyle's law of gases
summary: Robert Boyle published in 1662 the relation that the volume of a fixed quantity of gas varies inversely with its pressure at constant temperature. It was one of the first quantitative laws to come out of a designed experiment.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Boyle worked at Oxford with an air pump built for him by Robert Hooke, and used it to show that air has weight and springiness, that sound will not travel in a vacuum, and that neither a flame nor a small animal survives without it. The pressure–volume relation came from a different apparatus: a J-shaped glass tube in which poured mercury compressed a trapped column of air, so that pressure and volume could both be read off and compared. The idea had been put to him by Richard Towneley and Henry Power, which Boyle acknowledged in print; on the Continent the same law is often credited to Edme Mariotte.

*The Sceptical Chymist* (1661) attacked the four Aristotelian elements and the alchemists' three principles alike, argued for treating matter as corpuscles, and insisted that chemical claims be settled by experiment. Boyle also insisted on describing apparatus and procedure in enough detail for others to repeat the work, including experiments that failed.

A founder member of the Royal Society, he stands between alchemy and chemistry, since he pursued transmutation as well. His law later became one leg of the ideal gas law.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyle%27s_law).

name: Robert Hooke discovers cells
summary: Robert Hooke's *Micrographia*, published in 1665, showed readers what a microscope could see. Examining a slice of cork, he found it divided into small compartments and called them cells, the word biology still uses.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). *Micrographia* was the Royal Society's first popular success: a large illustrated book with fold-out engravings drawn by Hooke himself of a flea, a louse, the compound eye of a fly, and the point of a needle looking blunt and ragged under magnification. Samuel Pepys sat up until two in the morning with it and called it the most ingenious book he had ever read.

The cork observation was of dead plant tissue: what Hooke saw were the empty walls left behind by cells, and he named them for their likeness to the cells of a monastery. He did not suppose they were the units of life. That idea came in the 1830s with Schleiden and Schwann, and later Virchow, and it needed the better microscopes of the nineteenth century.

Hooke was the Society's curator of experiments, obliged to produce several demonstrations a week, and worked on springs (the law of elasticity is his), on gravitation, on fossils as remains of once-living things, and on rebuilding London as a surveyor after the fire of 1666. His long quarrel with [Newton](event:newton) over priority in the inverse-square law left him a marginal figure for two centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hooke).

name: Calculus
summary: The mathematics of change: differentiation, which measures rates, integration, which accumulates them, and the theorem that the two are inverse operations.
body:
Areas and tangents had been attacked for two thousand years, by Archimedes with exhaustion arguments and by Fermat, Cavalieri and Barrow with methods that worked case by case. What [Newton](item:isaac-newton) and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz supplied in the 1660s and 1670s was a general calculus: a notation and a set of rules that made the problems routine, and the fundamental theorem linking the two operations.

Newton developed his fluxions first and used them in the *[Principia](item:newton)*, though he presented the results there in classical geometry. Leibniz published first, and his notation, dx, dy and the integral sign, is the one still in use. The priority dispute between them, and between their national followers, lasted decades.

The foundations were shaky for a century and a half: infinitesimals were quantities that had to be non-zero and then zero, an objection Bishop Berkeley put memorably. Cauchy and Weierstrass replaced them with limits in the nineteenth century. By then the calculus had become the standard language of physics and engineering, and the basis of the differential equations used to describe continuous processes.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus).

name: Great Fire of London
summary: A fire that burned through the City of London from 2 to 6 September 1666, destroying about 13,200 houses, 87 churches and St Paul's Cathedral.
body:
The fire began in a bakery in Pudding Lane in the early hours of Sunday 2 September 1666, after a dry summer and with a strong east wind. The medieval City was built of timber and pitch with jettied upper storeys, and warehouses along the Thames held oil, tallow, spirits and coal.

The lord mayor refused to order demolitions early on, and by the time firebreaks were made with gunpowder the fire had a front too wide to hold. It burned for four days, destroyed about 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches, the Royal Exchange, the Guildhall and old St Paul's Cathedral, and left an area of about 1.75 square kilometres inside the walls in ruins.

Recorded deaths were very few, though the count only covered those whose deaths were registered. Around 70,000 of the City's 80,000 inhabitants lost their homes. Rebuilding was regulated by the Act of 1667, which required brick and stone and widened streets, and [Christopher Wren](event:wren-cathedral) rebuilt St Paul's and 51 parish churches.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Fire_of_London).

name: Leeuwenhoek's microscopes reveal microorganisms
summary: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a draper in Delft, made single-lens microscopes that magnified up to about 270 times and used them from 1674 to describe protozoa, bacteria, sperm cells and red blood cells.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). His instruments were not the compound microscopes [Hooke](event:hooke-cells) used but small brass plates holding a single tiny, almost spherical lens, with the specimen mounted on a pin in front of it. They were awkward to use and better than anything else for a century and a half. He ground and mounted the lenses himself and never disclosed his best method; of the several hundred he made, about a dozen survive.

In 1674 he reported "animalcules" swimming in lake water. In 1676 he described much smaller ones, bacteria, in an infusion of pepper and in scrapings from his own teeth. He also described spermatozoa, the banding of striated muscle, yeast cells, and blood corpuscles passing single file through capillaries, which supplied the link [Harvey](event:harvey-circulation) had been unable to see.

He had no Latin and no university training and wrote in Dutch, sending some 190 letters to the Royal Society in London. His claims were so implausible that the Society sent independent observers to verify them before electing him a fellow in 1680. Nothing connected the creatures he found to disease until [germ theory](event:germ-theory), two centuries later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonie_van_Leeuwenhoek).

name: Maratha Empire
summary: An Indian state founded by Shivaji in 1674 that grew into the dominant power in eighteenth century India, before losing to the East India Company in three wars ending in 1818.
body:
The Maratha state was founded in the western Deccan by Shivaji, who was crowned at Raigad in 1674 after twenty years of war against the sultanate of Bijapur and the [Mughals](event:mughal-empire). Its base was the hill forts of the Sahyadri range and a light cavalry that lived off enemy territory.

[Aurangzeb](event:aurangzeb-reign) spent the last twenty-five years of his reign in the Deccan trying to destroy it and did not succeed. In the eighteenth century, under the hereditary chief ministers known as the peshwas, the Marathas collected tribute across much of India, occupied Delhi's politics and reached the Indus.

The confederacy of ruling families, Bhonsle, Holkar, Scindia, Gaekwad and the peshwa, was checked at [Panipat](event:third-panipat) in 1761 by Ahmad Shah Durrani and recovered within a decade. Three wars with the [East India Company](event:english-east-india) between 1775 and 1818 ended with the peshwa's deposition and the annexation of most of the territory.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratha_Empire).

name: Christopher Wren builds St. Paul's Cathedral
summary: Christopher Wren designed a new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of London destroyed the medieval church in 1666. It was built between 1675 and 1711, and its dome is one of the largest in the world.
body:
Wren was an astronomer and mathematician, a founder of the Royal Society, who turned to architecture in his thirties. His first designs for St Paul's were rejected: the Great Model of 1673, a centralised Greek cross, offended clergy who wanted a long nave for processions. The warrant design he was finally granted he then altered extensively under a clause allowing him to make "ornamental" changes as he went, which is how the built church came to differ so much from the approved drawings.

The dome is built as three shells: an inner one shaped for the view from the floor, a brick cone in the middle that carries the stone lantern, and a timber-and-lead outer dome for the skyline, with an iron chain around the base to take the outward thrust. The stone is Portland, shipped from Dorset. Wren was paid partly from a duty on coal entering London, and he lived to see it finished, being hauled up in a basket to inspect the work in his old age.

He also designed fifty-one City parish churches after the fire, whose varied steeples gave London its skyline, and worked at Greenwich, Chelsea and Hampton Court. He is buried in the crypt of St Paul's beneath an inscription that tells the reader who seeks his monument to look around.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul%27s_Cathedral).

name: Peter the Great modernizes Russia
summary: Peter I ruled Russia from 1682 to 1725 and forced on it a programme of Western-style reform: a navy, a modern army, a reorganised state and church, and a new capital at St Petersburg. He defeated Sweden and made Russia a European great power.
body:
Peter travelled to the Dutch Republic and England in 1697–98 with a "Grand Embassy", working in shipyards under a thin pretence of anonymity to learn the trade. He came home to crush a revolt of the streltsy, the old Moscow guard, with torture and mass public executions, and then set about remaking the state: a Table of Ranks tying noble status to service rather than birth, new provincial governments, a Senate, administrative colleges on the Swedish model, and the abolition of the patriarchate in favour of a synod under a lay official. He taxed almost everything, beards included.

The Great Northern War against Sweden ran from 1700 to 1721. Beaten at Narva at the outset, he rebuilt the army around conscription and artillery and won decisively at Poltava in 1709; the Treaty of Nystad gave Russia the eastern Baltic coast, and he took the title of emperor. His campaigns against the Ottomans went much less well.

[St Petersburg](event:st-petersburg-founded), begun in 1703 on captured marshland, became the capital in 1712 and was built with conscripted labour at heavy cost in lives. The reforms were imposed from above and paid for by a peasantry whose serfdom deepened under them; his son Alexei died under interrogation for opposing them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_the_Great).

name: Ottoman siege of Vienna
summary: An Ottoman army besieged Vienna from July 1683. On 12 September a relief force led by John III Sobieski of Poland broke the siege in a battle outside the city. It was the last Ottoman attempt on Vienna and the beginning of a long retreat from central Europe.
body:
Part of [Ottoman wars in Europe](event:ottoman-wars-europe). The grand vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha brought perhaps 100,000 men up the Danube. The emperor Leopold I left the city, whose garrison of about 15,000 under Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg held walls that Ottoman sappers mined steadily from trenches driven up to the ditch. By early September the defences were breached in places, the food was gone and dysentery was spreading.

A relief army assembled under a treaty between Leopold and Poland-Lithuania, brokered and part-funded by Pope Innocent XI: Polish, Saxon, Bavarian and imperial contingents, about 70,000 men, with Sobieski in overall command. They came down from the wooded Kahlenberg heights north-west of the city on 12 September and fought their way through the Ottoman flank. The action ended with what is usually described as the largest cavalry charge in history, some 18,000 horse including the Polish winged hussars, and the Ottoman camp was taken. Kara Mustafa was executed at Belgrade on the sultan's orders that December.

A Holy League followed up the victory and took Hungary over the next fifteen years. The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 was the first in which the Ottomans ceded substantial territory, and Austria became the dominant power in central Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vienna).

name: J.S. Bach's compositions
summary: Johann Sebastian Bach worked as an organist, court musician and church cantor in provincial Germany and wrote well over a thousand pieces. He is generally regarded as the summit of baroque music, though his reputation came a century after his death.
body:
Bach was born at Eisenach into a family that had supplied musicians to Thuringia for generations, and held posts at Arnstadt, Weimar and Cöthen before becoming Cantor of the Thomasschule in Leipzig in 1723, where he stayed for the rest of his life. The Leipzig job required new music for most Sundays of the church year: he wrote some 300 cantatas, of which about 200 survive, along with the *St Matthew* and *St John* Passions and the Mass in B minor.

The instrumental music was often written for teaching or for a particular employer: the *Brandenburg Concertos*, offered to a margrave who seems never to have had them played; the *Well-Tempered Clavier*, two sets of preludes and fugues in all twenty-four keys; the cello suites; the *Goldberg Variations*; and *The Art of Fugue*, left unfinished. The technique is contrapuntal: several independent voices, each a melody, which together make the harmony. He never travelled outside Germany.

In his lifetime he was known chiefly as an organ virtuoso, and by the time he died in 1750 his style was thought old-fashioned. Mendelssohn's performance of the *St Matthew Passion* in 1829 began the revival, and a complete edition followed later in the century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach).

name: The Enlightenment
summary: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement of the long eighteenth century which held that reason, evidence and free criticism should decide any claim, whether about nature, religion or government. It ran from roughly the 1680s to the end of the century, centred on France, Britain, Scotland and the German states.
body:
Its confidence came from the [new science](event:scientific-revolution): if the heavens obeyed laws that a person could work out, so might society.
