Locke argued that knowledge comes from experience and that government rests on consent and may be dissolved; [Montesquieu](event:montesquieu-spirit) analysed how power might be divided so that it checks itself; [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment) attacked judicial cruelty, censorship and clerical privilege; [Hume](event:hume-philosophy) pressed empiricism to sceptical conclusions; [Rousseau](event:rousseau-social) dissented from much of it, holding that civilisation corrupts; [Adam Smith](event:wealth-of-nations) described a commercial society ordered without anyone directing it; Kant answered the question "what is enlightenment?" with the motto *sapere aude*, dare to know.

It was carried by print and by sociability rather than by universities: the [*Encyclopédie*](event:diderot-encyclopedia), pamphlets, cheap pirated reprints, coffee houses, Parisian salons run by women, provincial academies and masonic lodges. Much of it was printed abroad or clandestinely to evade the censors. Beccaria's argument against torture and the death penalty, and the campaign against the [slave trade](event:slave-trade), show what it produced in practice.

Its politics were not uniform: some looked to reforming monarchs ([enlightened absolutism](event:enlightened-despotism)), others to representative government. Its language of natural rights and popular sovereignty passed into the [American](event:american-revolution) and [French](event:french-revolution) revolutions. Critics from the Romantics onward charged it with a thin view of tradition, feeling and community, and with a universalism that in practice excluded women, the poor and the colonised.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment).

name: Newton's Principia
summary: Isaac Newton's *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, published in 1687, set out three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation. A single set of principles accounted for falling bodies, the tides, the paths of comets and the orbits of the planets.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). The book was written in about eighteen months after Edmond Halley asked [Newton](item:isaac-newton) what curve a planet would follow under an inverse-square attraction and was told, from memory, an ellipse; Newton had worked it out years earlier and mislaid the proof. Halley paid for the printing himself.

The first law says a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a force acts on it; the second relates force to change of motion; the third pairs every action with an equal and opposite reaction. Gravitation is universal: every mass attracts every other in proportion to the product of the masses and inversely as the square of the distance between them. From these Newton derived [Kepler's laws](event:kepler), explained the tides by the pull of Moon and Sun, showed why the Earth bulges at the equator, and made comets predictable, a prediction Halley's comet kept in 1758.

The argument is presented in classical geometry rather than in the [calculus](item:calculus) Newton had invented and used, which is one reason the book is so hard. He declined to say what gravity *is*, writing *hypotheses non fingo*, I feign no hypotheses, and gave only the law by which it acts, an omission Continental followers of Descartes attacked for decades as a return to occult qualities. The *Principia* set the standard the sciences aimed at for two hundred years, until [relativity](event:relativity) showed the limits of its account of gravity without displacing it as a working theory.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophiæ_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica).

name: Glorious Revolution
summary: In November 1688 William of Orange landed in England at the invitation of leading politicians, and James II fled to France. Parliament declared the throne vacant, made William and Mary joint monarchs, and passed a Bill of Rights that fixed the limits of royal power.
body:
James II was Catholic, and had been tolerated on the expectation that his Protestant daughter Mary would succeed him. He suspended penal laws by prerogative, placed Catholics in the army, the universities and the government, and prosecuted seven bishops who petitioned against him. The birth of a son in June 1688 promised a Catholic dynasty instead, and seven peers and bishops wrote to William, Mary's husband and the Dutch stadtholder, inviting him to intervene.

William crossed with a large fleet and about 15,000 troops. James's army melted away, his nerve failed, and he was deliberately allowed to escape, which let Parliament treat the throne as abandoned rather than seized. The settlement of 1689 required the monarch to be Protestant, forbade a standing army or taxation without parliamentary consent, guaranteed frequent elections and free speech in Parliament, and barred the suspending of laws. A Toleration Act gave Protestant dissenters freedom of worship.

It was neither bloodless nor purely English. It brought England into William's war against Louis XIV, which required regular parliaments to vote money and led to the Bank of England in 1694 and a permanent funded national debt. In Ireland and Scotland it was decided by fighting, including the Boyne in 1690, and left a Jacobite cause that lasted until 1746.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glorious_Revolution).

name: Voltaire's philosophy and writings
summary: Voltaire was the most widely read French writer of the eighteenth century and the Enlightenment's most effective polemicist. He attacked religious intolerance, censorship and judicial cruelty in poems, plays, histories, letters and short satirical tales.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Born François-Marie Arouet, he was imprisoned in the Bastille at twenty-two for verses against the regent, and later beaten by a nobleman's servants and exiled for answering back. Two and a half years in England left him an admirer of its religious toleration, its constitution and [Newton](event:newton), whose physics he did much to popularise in France; his *Lettres philosophiques* of 1734 used English practice as a rebuke to French, and was burned by the public hangman.

He wrote tragedies, an epic, a history of the age of Louis XIV, an *Essay on Customs* that took in China and the Islamic world, and articles for the [*Encyclopédie*](event:diderot-encyclopedia). *Candide* (1759) mocked the doctrine that this is the best of all possible worlds, a target sharpened by the [Lisbon earthquake](event:lisbon-earthquake).

From Ferney, an estate near the Swiss border he could cross if the police came, he ran campaigns for the victims of judicial persecution, above all Jean Calas, a Protestant broken on the wheel in 1762 on a false charge of murdering his son, whose conviction Voltaire got quashed posthumously. *Écrasez l'infâme*, crush the infamous thing, meant clerical and judicial persecution rather than religion as such: he was a deist, and no democrat.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire).

name: Founding of the Bank of England
summary: The Bank of England was chartered on 27 July 1694 to lend 1.2 million pounds to the government, establishing the funded national debt.
body:
The Bank was set up during the Nine Years' War, when the English government could not borrow enough on the terms available. Subscribers put up 1,200,000 pounds, lent the whole sum to the crown at 8 per cent, and received a charter allowing them to issue notes and take deposits.

The arrangement made the debt an obligation of parliament rather than of the monarch, which is why lenders accepted it after the [Glorious Revolution](event:glorious-revolution) had made parliament's control of taxation permanent. Interest rates on government borrowing fell over the following decades to about half those paid by France.

The Bank managed the debt, issued notes that circulated as money in London, and became the model for later central banks. Britain's capacity to borrow, rather than the size of its population or revenue, is the usual explanation for how it sustained the eighteenth century wars against larger states.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England).

name: Great Northern War
summary: A war fought from 1700 to 1721 in which a coalition led by Russia, Denmark and Saxony-Poland ended Swedish supremacy in the Baltic. Russia gained Estonia, Livonia and Ingria.
body:
The Great Northern War was fought between 1700 and 1721 between Sweden and a coalition of Russia, Denmark-Norway and Saxony-Poland, later joined by Prussia and Hanover. It decided which state would dominate the Baltic.

The allies attacked in 1700, expecting an easy war against an eighteen year old king. Charles XII knocked Denmark out in weeks, destroyed a much larger Russian army at [Narva](event:narva) in November, and then spent six years in Poland forcing Augustus II off the throne. [Peter I](event:peter-the-great) used the time to rebuild his army on European lines, take Ingria and found St Petersburg.

Charles invaded Russia in 1708, turned south into Ukraine, lost his supply train at Lesnaya and his army at [Poltava](event:poltava) in July 1709. He spent five years in Ottoman territory while Russia occupied the Baltic provinces and Finland.

Charles was killed besieging Fredriksten in Norway in 1718. The treaty of Nystad in 1721 gave Russia Estonia, Livonia, Ingria and part of Karelia, and Peter took the title of emperor. Sweden's period as a great power was over.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_War).

steps.name: Three allies against Sweden
steps.page:
Saxony, Denmark and Russia agreed to partition the Swedish Baltic provinces while Charles XII was fifteen. Augustus II of Saxony and Poland attacked Riga in February 1700 and Denmark invaded Holstein-Gottorp.

Charles answered Denmark first. With an Anglo-Dutch squadron covering the crossing, he landed at Humlebaek near Copenhagen in August, and Denmark left the war by the peace of Travendal on 18 August. He then shipped his army to Livonia.

steps.name: Six years in Poland
steps.page:
Charles XII turned on Augustus II rather than on Russia. He crossed the Duna in 1701, took Warsaw and Krakow in 1702, beat the Saxon and Polish army at Kliszow on 19 July 1702 and at Pultusk in 1703, and had Stanislaw Leszczynski elected king in 1704.

The war was finished by an invasion of Saxony itself: at Altranstadt in September 1706 Augustus renounced the Polish crown and his alliance with Russia. The six years bought Peter I the time in which he rebuilt his army, took Ingria and founded [St Petersburg](event:st-petersburg-founded) in 1703.

layers.label: Charles XII into Poland and Saxony

steps.name: The march into Russia
steps.page:
Charles XII left Saxony at the end of 1707 with about 44,000 men, crossed the Vistula and the Berezina, and beat the Russians at Holowczyn on 14 July 1708. The Russian army fell back, burning the country and the stores in front of him.

Instead of marching on Moscow he turned south into Ukraine, expecting supplies and the support of the hetman Ivan Mazepa. The supply column and reinforcement coming from Riga under Lewenhaupt was destroyed at Lesnaya on 9 October, and the winter of 1708 to 1709 was the coldest in living memory.

steps.name: Russia takes the Baltic
steps.page:
With the Swedish field army gone, Peter I took Riga, Reval and Vyborg in 1710 and moved into Finland in 1713. On 7 August 1714 the Russian galley fleet beat a Swedish squadron off Hango in the first significant Russian naval victory.

Charles XII, meanwhile, spent five years in Ottoman territory at Bender, where he pressed the sultan into a war with Russia; Peter was surrounded on the Prut in 1711 and bought his way out by returning Azov. Charles rode back to Swedish Pomerania in 1714.

steps.name: Fredriksten and Nystad
steps.page:
Charles XII returned to a country stripped of men and money, and invaded Norway twice. He was shot dead in the trenches before Fredriksten on 30 November 1718; whether the shot came from the fortress has been argued over ever since.

Sweden made peace with Hanover, Prussia and Denmark in 1719 and 1720, and with Russia at Nystad on 10 September 1721, giving up Livonia, Estonia, Ingria and part of Karelia. Peter took the title of emperor the same year. Sweden's period as a great power ended; Russia's began.

name: Battle of Narva
summary: A Swedish army of about 10,000 under Charles XII routed a Russian force several times its size besieging Narva on 30 November 1700.
body:
Part of [Great Northern War](event:great-northern-war). Peter I had invested Narva in Swedish Ingria with an army usually given as around 35,000 men, spread along nearly seven kilometres of siege lines. Charles XII landed in Pernau and marched to relieve the place with about 10,000.

He attacked on the afternoon of 30 November during a snowstorm that blew into the Russian faces and hid the approach. The Swedish columns broke through the lines in two places within a quarter of an hour and rolled them up. The Russian foreign officers surrendered; a bridge collapsed under the retreat; the guns were lost.

Charles concluded that Russia was beaten and turned against Poland. Peter rebuilt his army, casting new guns from church bells, and took the coast of the Gulf of Finland within three years. Narva itself fell to him in 1704.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Narva_(1700)).

name: Ashanti Empire
summary: An Akan state in what is now Ghana, founded about 1701 around Kumasi, which controlled the gold and kola trade of the forest zone and fought Britain in a series of wars.
body:
The Ashanti state was formed about 1701 when Osei Tutu united the Akan chiefdoms of the forest around Kumasi and defeated Denkyira, which had held the region tributary. Its symbol of unity was the Golden Stool, said to have been called down by the priest Okomfo Anokye, which no one sat on and which represented the nation rather than a king.

The empire lived on gold, kola nuts and the trade in captives to the coast, exchanged for firearms and manufactured goods. It ran a road network out of Kumasi, a standing bureaucracy with appointed rather than hereditary officials in key posts, and an army raised by levy on the provinces.

Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and the two powers then competed over the coastal states. Four Anglo-Ashanti wars were fought between 1824 and 1900; Kumasi was occupied and burned in 1874, the asantehene was deported in 1896, and after the rising of 1900, in which Yaa Asantewaa led the defence of the Golden Stool, the territory was annexed in 1902.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashanti_Empire).

name: War of the Spanish Succession
summary: A European war fought from 1701 to 1714 over the succession to the Spanish monarchy. Philip V kept Spain and its American empire; Britain and Austria took the territory and the trade concessions settled at Utrecht.
body:
Charles II of Spain died in 1700 without an heir, leaving the Spanish monarchy, which included the Netherlands, Milan, Naples, Sicily and the Americas, to Philip of Anjou, a grandson of Louis XIV. The other powers had spent a decade negotiating partition treaties to avoid exactly this, and the union of the French and Spanish crowns was not acceptable to them.

England, the Dutch republic and the Emperor formed the Grand Alliance and fought in the Low Countries, on the Danube, in Italy and in Spain. The allied commanders, the duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy, won at [Blenheim](event:blenheim) in 1704, Ramillies in 1706, Oudenarde in 1708 and Malplaquet in 1709.

In Spain itself the Bourbon claimant held Castile and won at Almansa in 1707. When the Emperor Joseph I died in 1711 and his brother Charles, the allied candidate for Spain, inherited Austria, Britain lost interest in the original aim and opened separate talks.

The treaties of Utrecht in 1713 and Rastatt in 1714 confirmed Philip V in Spain on condition that the two crowns stayed separate, gave Britain Gibraltar, Minorca and the asiento, and transferred the Spanish possessions in Italy and the Netherlands to Austria.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Spanish_Succession).

steps.name: The alliance and the outbreak
steps.page:
Charles II of Spain died childless in November 1700, leaving the whole monarchy by will to Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV. Louis accepted the will rather than the partition treaties he had signed, sent French troops into the Spanish Netherlands, and registered Philip's continuing rights to the French succession.

England, the Dutch republic and the Emperor renewed the Grand Alliance in September 1701 and declared war in May 1702. The fighting ran in four theatres: the Low Countries, the upper Rhine and Danube, Italy, and Spain.

steps.name: Ramillies and Turin
steps.page:
An Anglo-Dutch force took Gibraltar in August 1704 and it was held against a siege the following year. In 1706 the allies won in two theatres in one summer.

Marlborough broke the French army at Ramillies on 23 May and took Brussels, Antwerp, Ghent and Bruges within weeks, so that most of the Spanish Netherlands changed hands in a single campaign. On 7 September Prince Eugene and the duke of Savoy relieved Turin, and the French withdrew from northern Italy.

steps.name: The war in Spain
steps.page:
The allies backed the Habsburg claimant, Charles, and landed in Portugal and Catalonia. Barcelona was taken in 1705 and Madrid was occupied twice, in 1706 and 1710, and given up each time because Castile supported Philip V.

A Bourbon army under the duke of Berwick destroyed the allied field army at Almansa on 25 April 1707, and the defeats at Brihuega and Villaviciosa in December 1710 ended the allied position outside Catalonia. When the Emperor Joseph died in 1711 and Charles inherited Austria, the war aim of putting him on the Spanish throne lost its point in London.

steps.name: Oudenarde, Lille and Malplaquet
steps.page:
A French offensive in Flanders retook Ghent and Bruges in 1708 and was beaten at Oudenarde on 11 July in a meeting engagement fought as the armies arrived. The allies then besieged Lille, the strongest fortress of Vauban's belt, and took the town in October and the citadel in December.

France was by then in a subsistence crisis after the winter of 1709 and offered terms which the allies raised beyond what Louis XIV would grant. The campaign of 1709 ended at Malplaquet on 11 September, an allied victory with about 20,000 casualties among the winners, the heaviest of the war.

steps.name: Denain and Utrecht
steps.page:
A change of ministry in London in 1710 turned British policy towards peace, and in 1712 the British contingent was withdrawn from the allied army in the field. Villars caught the Dutch and Austrian force at Denain on 24 July 1712 and beat it, then retook the fortresses lost since 1708.

The treaties signed at Utrecht on 11 April 1713 left Philip V king of Spain and the Indies on condition that the crowns of France and Spain were never united. Britain took Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, Acadia and the asiento contract for supplying slaves to Spanish America; Austria took the Spanish Netherlands, Milan, Naples and Sardinia. The Emperor made his own peace at Rastatt in 1714.

name: Founding of St. Petersburg
summary: Peter the Great founded St Petersburg in May 1703 on marshland at the mouth of the Neva, on ground just taken from Sweden. It became the Russian capital in 1712 and remained so until 1918.
body:
Part of [Peter the Great](event:peter-the-great)'s remaking of Russia. The site was chosen for access to the Baltic, not for comfort: flat, flooded, freezing, with no stone and no local labour. Tens of thousands of conscripted peasants, soldiers and Swedish prisoners were sent north each year to drive piles and dig canals, and large numbers died of disease, cold and exhaustion. The city has been called one built on bones, though the figures are not documented.

Peter had it laid out on a European plan by Italian, French and German architects: straight avenues, granite embankments, the Peter and Paul Fortress, the Admiralty shipyard, and later the Winter Palace. Nobles were ordered to build houses there and merchants to trade through the port, and stone building was banned elsewhere in Russia for a time so that masons would have to come.

It was Russia's window on the West, its chief port and the seat of its court, and by 1900 one of the largest cities in Europe and the centre of its literature, music and revolutionary politics. It was renamed Petrograd in 1914, Leningrad in 1924, and St Petersburg again in 1991.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg).

name: Battle of Blenheim
summary: Marlborough and Eugene destroyed a Franco-Bavarian army on the Danube on 13 August 1704, ending the threat to Vienna and the run of French victories.
body:
Part of [War of the Spanish Succession](event:war-spanish-succession). A French and Bavarian army was within reach of Vienna in 1704 and the Emperor was also facing a rising in Hungary. Marlborough marched his army about 400 kilometres from the Low Countries to the Danube in five weeks, keeping the destination hidden from friend and enemy, and joined Prince Eugene.

The armies met near the village of Blindheim on 13 August. Marlborough pinned the French wings, one of them packed into the village itself, and broke through the weakened centre with cavalry in the late afternoon. The French commander Tallard was captured. Franco-Bavarian losses were about 30,000 killed, wounded and taken.

Bavaria left the war and Vienna was safe. The battle ended the reputation of invincibility the French army had held since the 1640s, and Queen Anne gave Marlborough the manor of Woodstock, where Blenheim Palace was built.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Blenheim).

name: Act of Union creates Great Britain
summary: The Acts of Union passed by the English and Scottish parliaments in 1706 and 1707 joined the two kingdoms into one, called Great Britain, with a single parliament at Westminster from 1 May 1707.
body:
The crowns had been shared since James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne in 1603, but the kingdoms kept separate parliaments, and by 1700 the arrangement was breaking down. Scotland's parliament asserted a right to choose a different successor to Queen Anne; England, at war with France, could not accept a separate Scottish foreign policy on its northern border. The failure of the Darién scheme, a Scottish attempt at a colony in Panama that swallowed a large share of the country's liquid capital, made access to English colonial markets attractive to those who had lost money, and the compensation fund written into the treaty, the *Equivalent*, went largely to them.

The treaty gave Scotland 45 seats in the Commons and 16 elected peers in the Lords, free trade within the union and its empire, and the retention of its own legal system, courts, burghs and Presbyterian church. It was unpopular in the streets of Edinburgh and Glasgow and was carried in the Scottish parliament by a majority its opponents said had been bought; Burns later wrote of a nation "bought and sold for English gold".

The union held. Jacobite risings in 1715 and 1745 failed to undo it, and Scots took a large part in British trade, empire, science and the Enlightenment that followed. Scottish independence was rejected in a referendum in 2014.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707).

name: Battle of Poltava
summary: Peter I destroyed the Swedish field army under Charles XII at Poltava in Ukraine on 8 July 1709. It is the usual marker for the end of Swedish and the beginning of Russian predominance in northern Europe.
body:
Part of [Great Northern War](event:great-northern-war). Charles XII had wintered in Ukraine with an army reduced by cold, hunger and the loss of the Lewenhaupt supply column at Lesnaya. In May 1709 he laid siege to Poltava on the Vorskla, and in June he was wounded in the foot and could not take the field in person.

Peter I came up with about 45,000 men and built a line of redoubts across the approach. The Swedish attack on the morning of 8 July, with roughly 20,000 men and almost no artillery ammunition, broke up among the redoubts, and the second phase was fought against an army twice its size in the open. The survivors surrendered at Perevolochna three days later.

Charles escaped with Mazepa into Ottoman territory and spent five years at Bender. Denmark and Saxony rejoined the war, Russia took the Baltic provinces, and the balance in northern Europe did not change back.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poltava).

name: South Sea Bubble
summary: A speculative rise and collapse in the shares of the South Sea Company in London in 1720, following a scheme to exchange the company's stock for government debt.
body:
The South Sea Company was founded in 1711 to trade with Spanish America and, more importantly, to take over part of the British national debt in exchange for shares and an annuity from the government. Its trading rights, obtained at [Utrecht](event:war-spanish-succession) in 1713, amounted to one ship a year and the asiento contract for supplying slaves.

In 1720 the company agreed to convert most of the remaining national debt. The higher its share price, the less stock it had to give holders of debt, so the directors lent money to buyers of their own shares and spread favourable reports. The price rose from about 100 pounds in January to about 1,000 in August and fell back to roughly its starting level by December.

A parliamentary inquiry found bribes paid to ministers and to members of the royal household. Robert Walpole managed the settlement and emerged as the leading minister. The Bubble Act of 1720, which restricted the formation of joint-stock companies without a charter, remained in force until 1825.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sea_Bubble).

name: Yongzheng Emperor's Qing reforms
summary: The Yongzheng Emperor ruled the Qing for thirteen years from 1722. He centralised decision-making, attacked corruption, reformed the tax system and left a full treasury. His reign falls between his father Kangxi's conquests and his son Qianlong's long reign.
body:
Part of [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). He came to the throne in disputed circumstances after the long succession struggle among [Kangxi](event:kangxi-emperor)'s sons, and dealt with his surviving brothers harshly, imprisoning several. He worked prodigiously, reading and annotating memorials late into the night in his own hand.

The palace memorial system let chosen officials write to the emperor directly and in secret, bypassing the bureaucracy that would otherwise have edited the report, which made provincial governors individually accountable. He created what became the Grand Council, a small inner body for urgent business. He merged the head tax into the land tax, so that liability fell on land rather than on people, and legalised a surcharge that had long been collected informally, using it to pay officials a "salary to nourish honesty" instead of leaving them to live on fees. He also freed several hereditary outcast groups from their debased legal status.

In the south-west he replaced hereditary native chieftains with regular officials, at the cost of years of fighting. The scholar-elite whose latitude he curtailed disliked him, and his historical reputation suffered accordingly; the state he handed on in 1735 was solvent and tightly run.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongzheng_Emperor).

name: Qianlong Emperor
summary: The Qianlong Emperor reigned from 1735 to 1796 over the Qing at its greatest extent, conquered Dzungaria and Xinjiang, and commissioned the Siku Quanshu literary collection.
body:
Part of [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). Qianlong, grandson of the [Kangxi Emperor](event:kangxi-emperor), reigned from 1735 to 1796 and then abdicated in order not to rule longer than his grandfather, keeping power until his death in 1799.

His campaigns, presented later as the Ten Great Campaigns, doubled the territory of the empire. The Dzungar khanate in the north west was destroyed between 1755 and 1758; the region was renamed Xinjiang and settled. Modern historians describe the destruction of the Dzungars, in which a large part of the population died in the fighting and in the smallpox that followed, as a genocide.

The reign was also a peak of population growth, of trade through Canton, and of state-sponsored scholarship. The Siku Quanshu, compiled from 1772, collected some 3,500 works and in the process censored or destroyed many others. In 1793 the Macartney embassy from Britain was received and its requests for open trade refused.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qianlong_Emperor).

name: Hume's empiricist philosophy
summary: David Hume, a Scottish philosopher and historian, argued that all knowledge comes from experience, and pressed the argument to sceptical conclusions: that causation is a habit of expectation rather than something observed, and that reason alone cannot tell anyone what to do.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). *A Treatise of Human Nature* appeared in 1739–40, when Hume was in his twenties, and in his own words "fell dead-born from the press". He recast its arguments in the *Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding* (1748) and the *Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals* (1751), which he thought his best work.

Three arguments have kept their force. On induction: no amount of past regularity gives a logical reason to expect the future to resemble it, so the expectation rests on custom rather than on proof. On causation: we observe one event constantly following another and never a necessary connection between them. On is and ought: a conclusion about what ought to be done cannot be derived from premises stating only what is, which Hume noted in a single paragraph that has been argued over ever since. He also denied that we have any impression of a continuing self, and in the posthumous *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion* dismantled the argument from design.

He was refused chairs at Edinburgh and Glasgow on suspicion of atheism and made his living as a librarian, diplomat and author of a best-selling *History of England*. Kant said Hume woke him from dogmatic slumber, and much of empiricism since has been a series of answers to his problems.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume).

name: Enlightened despotism in Prussia and Austria
summary: Several eighteenth-century monarchs, among them Frederick II of Prussia, Maria Theresa and Joseph II of Austria and Catherine II of Russia, adopted Enlightenment ideas about law, toleration and administration while keeping absolute power. The pattern is usually called enlightened absolutism.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Frederick took the throne in 1740, invaded Silesia within months, and spent much of his reign at war. He also abolished judicial torture, allowed broad religious toleration and a relatively free press, began the codification of Prussian law, and corresponded with [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment), who stayed three years at Potsdam before the friendship collapsed. Frederick called himself the first servant of the state.

Maria Theresa reformed taxation, the army and the central administration out of necessity after losing Silesia, and made primary schooling compulsory in 1774. Her son Joseph II went furthest and fastest: he abolished serfdom, issued a Patent of Toleration for Protestants, Orthodox and Jews, dissolved contemplative monasteries and used their funds for parishes and hospitals, imposed German as the language of administration everywhere, and legislated a single code. Almost all of it provoked revolt in Hungary and the Netherlands, and most was withdrawn at his death in 1790.

The reforms were made from above, in the interest of a stronger state as much as a freer subject: censorship, serfdom in Prussia and Russia, and noble privilege survived wherever they were useful. The phrase "everything for the people, nothing by the people" is a later summary of the position. The [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) exposed the tension, and most of these governments turned to repression afterwards.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlightened_absolutism).

name: War of the Austrian Succession
summary: A European war of 1740 to 1748 that began when Frederick II of Prussia invaded Silesia after Maria Theresa inherited the Habsburg lands. Prussia kept Silesia at the peace of Aix-la-Chapelle.
body:
Charles VI spent his reign persuading the European powers to accept the Pragmatic Sanction, which allowed his daughter Maria Theresa to inherit the Habsburg lands. He died in October 1740, and in December Frederick II of Prussia invaded Silesia, the richest Habsburg province, without a declaration of war.

France, Bavaria, Saxony and Spain joined against Austria, which was supported by Britain, Hanover and the Dutch republic. The elector of Bavaria was elected emperor in 1742, the first non-Habsburg in three centuries. Maria Theresa held the monarchy together by an appeal to the Hungarian diet and by keeping the army in the field.

Fighting spread to Italy, the Austrian Netherlands, where Marshal Saxe won at Fontenoy in 1745, and to North America and India, where it is known as King George's War and the First Carnatic War. A Jacobite rising in Britain in 1745 was part of the same conflict.

The peace of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748 restored most conquests and left Prussia with Silesia. Austria's attempt to recover it produced the [Seven Years' War](event:seven-years-war) eight years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Austrian_Succession).

name: Montesquieu's separation of powers
summary: Montesquieu's *The Spirit of the Laws*, published in 1748, argued that political liberty is preserved by dividing government into legislative, executive and judicial powers that check one another. It was among the most influential political books of the century.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Charles-Louis de Secondat, baron de Montesquieu, was a magistrate in Bordeaux who sold his office and spent twenty years on the book after travelling in Europe, including nearly two years in England. He had already made his name with the *Persian Letters* (1721), a satire of French society written in the voice of two Persian visitors.

The argument is comparative. Laws are not deduced from first principles but grow out of a people's climate, terrain, religion, commerce and manners, the "spirit" of the title, so that what suits one nation may ruin another. He classified governments as republics, monarchies and despotisms, each animated by its own principle: virtue, honour, fear. His model of separated powers was drawn from a reading of the English constitution that misdescribed it in places, and it was that reading which later writers followed.

The book was placed on the Index and went through many editions anyway. The framers of the [United States Constitution](event:us-constitution) cited him more than any other modern author. His climatic explanations of national character, and his chapter on slavery, written ironically and read straight by some, have worn much less well.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montesquieu).

name: Diderot's Encyclopédie
summary: The *Encyclopédie*, edited by Denis Diderot with Jean le Rond d'Alembert, appeared in Paris between 1751 and 1772: seventeen volumes of text and eleven of plates, some 72,000 articles by around 140 contributors. It was the great collective work of the Enlightenment.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). It began as a translation of an English cyclopedia and became something else: a survey of knowledge organised not by revelation but by the faculties of the human mind, with a system of cross-references that let a cautious article on an orthodox subject point the reader to a sceptical one elsewhere. Contributors included [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment), [Rousseau](event:rousseau-social), Montesquieu, Turgot and Quesnay; d'Alembert wrote the preliminary discourse and withdrew in 1759 under pressure.

Its treatment of the mechanical arts was deliberate and unusual. Diderot visited workshops, questioned craftsmen and had their tools and processes engraved in detail, on the argument that what a glassblower or a stocking-frame knitter knows deserves the same standing as what a bishop knows.

The privilege to publish was revoked in 1759 and the work continued semi-clandestinely with official knowledge; Diderot discovered late that his own publisher had been censoring the sheets behind his back. About 4,000 sets were sold before cheaper foreign reprints spread it much further. It made a body of critical, secular knowledge available to anyone who could afford a subscription, which is precisely what its enemies objected to.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclopédie).

name: Konbaung Dynasty unites Burma
summary: Alaungpaya founded the Konbaung dynasty in 1752 and reunified Burma after the collapse of the previous kingdom. Its rulers carried Burmese power to its greatest extent, and it was the last Burmese dynasty, ending with British annexation in 1885.
body:
The Restored Toungoo kingdom fell in 1752 to a rebellion from Lower Burma that took the capital at Ava. Alaungpaya, headman of a village near Shwebo, refused to submit, gathered a following, retook the country within five years, and destroyed the rival capital at Pegu in 1757. He founded Rangoon on the site of a fishing village near the mouth of the Irrawaddy.

His successors invaded Siam and sacked Ayutthaya in 1767, and between 1765 and 1769 fought off four invasions sent by the Qianlong Emperor. That war, expensive and unsuccessful for the Qing, was decided as much by malaria in the frontier hills as by battle. Later campaigns took Arakan in 1785 and Manipur and Assam in the following decades, carrying the Burmese frontier up to British Bengal.

Three Anglo-Burmese wars, in 1824–26, 1852 and 1885, took first the coastal provinces, then Lower Burma, then the rest; the first was among the most expensive wars the East India Company ever fought. King Thibaw was deported to India in 1885 and Burma became a province of British India.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konbaung_Dynasty).

name: Lisbon earthquake
summary: An earthquake estimated at magnitude 8.5 or more struck off the Portuguese coast on the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day. Shaking, a tsunami and fire destroyed most of Lisbon and killed tens of thousands of people.
body:
The shock came in several pulses over some minutes and opened fissures in the city centre. Survivors ran for the open ground of the waterfront; about forty minutes later the sea withdrew from the harbour and returned as a wave several metres high. Fires started by cooking hearths and by the candles lit in churches full for the feast day burned for days in what the water had not reached. Estimates of the dead in Lisbon range from about 12,000 to 50,000, and the tsunami also killed people in southern Portugal, Spain and Morocco.

The king's minister, later Marquis of Pombal, took charge with the instruction to bury the dead and feed the living. He hanged looters and rebuilt the lower town on a grid of standardised buildings framed in timber cages designed to flex, an early attempt at earthquake-resistant construction. He also circulated a questionnaire to every parish asking how long the shaking lasted, which way it ran, and how the wells and the sea behaved; the returns are a founding document of seismology.

The disaster struck a devout capital on a holy day, and forced the problem of evil into public argument. [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment) answered it in a poem and again in *Candide*; Rousseau replied that the deaths owed something to the decision to build seven storeys high.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake).

name: Mozart's compositions
summary: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed more than 600 works in thirty-five years, among them symphonies, concertos, operas, chamber and sacred music, and is one of the central figures of the classical style.
body:
He was a prodigy, exhibited across Europe by his father Leopold from the age of six, playing for courts in Munich, Paris, London and Vienna and absorbing every national style he met. He wrote his first symphony at eight and his first opera at eleven, and spent his twenties chafing at a post in Salzburg under an archbishop he detested, until he was dismissed in 1781, with a kick by his own account, and settled in Vienna.

There he worked freelance on subscription concerts, pupils, publication and commissions, which brought him a considerable income and no security at all. The mature work includes the last symphonies, numbers 39 to 41; the piano concertos he wrote to play himself; the six string quartets dedicated to Haydn, whom he admired and who admired him; and the operas *The Marriage of Figaro*, *Don Giovanni*, *Così fan tutte* and *The Magic Flute*, the first three to librettos by Lorenzo da Ponte.

He died in Vienna in December 1791, probably of an infectious illness, leaving the Requiem unfinished and debts his widow took years to clear. He was buried in a common grave, which was ordinary for the time and place; the story that Salieri poisoned him is a later legend.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart).

name: Seven Years' War
summary: The Seven Years' War was fought from 1756 to 1763 in Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, India and the Philippines. Britain and Prussia faced France, Austria, Russia and later Spain. Britain emerged with Canada and dominance in India; France lost most of its overseas empire.
body:
The alignment was new. Britain had been allied with Austria and France with Prussia; after the diplomatic revolution of 1756 the pairs swapped, and Austria set out to recover Silesia, which Frederick II of Prussia had seized in the previous war. Frederick struck first into Saxony. Fighting in North America had already begun in 1754, where the conflict is called the French and Indian War.

In Europe Prussia survived by interior lines, hard marching and Frederick's victories at Rossbach and Leuthen in 1757, and by British subsidies. It came close to collapse by 1761 and was saved when the Russian empress Elizabeth died and her successor, an admirer of Frederick, left the war. Overseas, sea power decided matters: Quebec fell in 1759, Montreal in 1760, the French posts in India by 1761, and Havana and Manila in 1762 after Spain entered.

The Peace of Paris in 1763 gave Britain Canada, Florida and predominance in India, where [Plassey](event:battle-plassey) had already put Bengal under the [East India Company](event:english-east-india). The Treaty of Hubertusburg restored the German boundaries and confirmed Prussia as a great power. Britain's war debt led it to tax its American colonies, and France's defeat and expense fed both its support for the [American Revolution](event:american-revolution) and the fiscal crisis behind the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). It is often described as the first global war.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years%27_War).

steps.name: Minorca and the invasion of Saxony
steps.page:
France opened the European war by taking Minorca in May 1756; the British admiral who failed to relieve it, John Byng, was court-martialled and shot on his own quarterdeck.

Frederick II struck first on land, marching into neutral Saxony in August, forcing the Saxon army to capitulate in October and pressing its soldiers into his own. The invasion gave his enemies a casus belli and gave him a base and a treasury.

steps.name: Rossbach and Leuthen
steps.page:
1757 nearly finished Prussia: Frederick was beaten at Kolín and invaded from three directions. Then in five weeks he destroyed a Franco-imperial army at Rossbach in November, marching his infantry across the enemy front, and an Austrian army twice his size at Leuthen in December.

Leuthen was fought by an oblique advance against one flank on ground he had drilled on in peacetime. The two victories kept Prussia in the war and made his military reputation across Europe.

steps.name: The year of victories
steps.page:
British and allied arms won everywhere in the second half of 1759. Minden in August stopped the French in Germany; Lagos and then Quiberon Bay in November wrecked the two French fleets and ended any prospect of invading Britain.

On 13 September Wolfe's army scaled the cliffs above Quebec and beat Montcalm on the Plains of Abraham; both commanders were killed, and the city surrendered days later. Montreal followed in 1760, ending French rule in Canada.

steps.name: Prussia's crisis and the Russian withdrawal
steps.page:
By 1761 Frederick had lost Silesian fortresses, Russian and Austrian armies had burned Berlin, his best troops were dead and Britain had stopped his subsidy. He carried poison and expected the end.

The Empress Elizabeth died in January 1762 and was succeeded by Peter III, an admirer who at once made peace and returned every conquest, the reversal Prussian historians called the miracle of the House of Brandenburg.

steps.name: Spain enters: Havana and Manila
steps.page:
Spain joined France in 1762 and lost two of its great colonial ports within months. A British expedition took Havana in August after a siege in which disease killed far more of the attackers than the fighting did.

A second force from Madras took Manila in October. Both were handed back at the peace, Havana in exchange for Florida, but the ease of their capture was noted everywhere.

steps.name: The Peace of Paris and Hubertusburg
steps.page:
By the Treaty of Paris on 10 February 1763 France ceded Canada and its territory east of the Mississippi to Britain, kept its sugar islands and its fishing rights, and abandoned political ambitions in India. Spain gave up Florida and received Louisiana from France.

Five days later the Treaty of Hubertusburg restored the German boundaries exactly as they had been: Prussia kept Silesia and no territory changed hands, after eight years of war.

name: Battle of Plassey
summary: On 23 June 1757 an East India Company force under Robert Clive defeated Siraj ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal, at Plassey north of Calcutta. The battle put Bengal under Company control and began British territorial rule in India.
body:
Part of [Seven Years' War](event:seven-years-war). The quarrel began when the young nawab took Calcutta in 1756, an episode remembered in Britain for the deaths of prisoners held overnight in the so-called Black Hole. Clive retook the city with a force from Madras. What followed was less a battle than the execution of a conspiracy: Clive, the Bengali banking house of Jagat Seth and other merchants had already agreed with Mir Jafar, the nawab's own commander, that he would hold back and be made nawab in his place.

Clive had about 3,000 men, two-thirds of them Indian sepoys, against perhaps 50,000. An afternoon rainstorm soaked the nawab's powder while the Company's guns, covered with tarpaulins, went on firing; Mir Jafar's large contingent never engaged. The fighting lasted a few hours and cost the Company around twenty dead. Siraj ud-Daulah fled and was killed days later.

Mir Jafar paid for his throne with enormous sums to the Company and to its officers individually; Clive took a personal fortune and was questioned about it in Parliament years afterwards. Victory at Buxar in 1764 confirmed the position, and in 1765 the Company obtained the *diwani*, the right to collect Bengal's revenue. From then the [Company](event:english-east-india) governed as well as traded.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Plassey).

name: Industrial Revolution
summary: From about 1760 Britain began making goods with machines driven by water and then by coal-fired steam, in factories rather than in households. Output per worker rose faster than population for the first time in history, and the pattern spread to western Europe, North America and eventually the world.
body:
Textiles came first, because spinning was the bottleneck: [the jenny, the water frame and the mule](event:spinning-jenny) multiplied what one worker could produce, and the work moved to where the power was. [Watt's engine](event:watt-engine), with its separate condenser and later its rotary drive, freed factories from riverbanks. Coke smelting and Cort's puddling process made cheap wrought iron; canals and then [railways](event:railways) carried coal, iron and cloth at a fraction of the old cost. Britain had the coal, the shipping, the colonial markets, the patent law and the capital, and historians still argue about which of those mattered most.

The social consequences arrived faster than any means of handling them. Manchester's population multiplied several times over in fifty years, into housing without drains or clean water, and life expectancy in the industrial towns was lower than in the countryside they drew on. Work was disciplined by the clock and the machine rather than by daylight and season. Children worked in mills and mines until the Factory Acts began restricting it from 1833. Handloom weavers were ruined; the Luddites broke frames in 1811–13; trade unions, the Chartist movement and a new vocabulary of class all came out of the same decades.

Sustained growth in output per head, energy use, urbanisation and population all begin their steep rise here, and so does the atmospheric carbon dioxide behind [modern climate change](event:global-warming).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution).

steps.name: Cromford and the factory system
steps.page:
Richard Arkwright's mill at Cromford, opened in 1771, ran water-powered frames day and night with a workforce of several hundred, many of them children, housed in a village built for them.

The organisation mattered as much as the machine: fixed hours, shifts, supervision and a discipline of the clock that had no precedent in the domestic workshops it replaced.

steps.name: Cheap iron: coke, puddling and the first iron bridge
steps.page:
Abraham Darby's family had smelted iron with coke rather than charcoal at Coalbrookdale since 1709, breaking the dependence on woodland. In 1779 the third Darby cast the world's first iron bridge over the Severn there.

Henry Cort's puddling and rolling process, patented in 1783–84, made wrought iron from pig iron with coal rather than charcoal and at many times the rate. Cheap iron made machines, rails, boilers and iron ships possible.

steps.name: Steam-powered cotton and the mule
steps.page:
The first Boulton and Watt rotative engine drove a cotton mill at Papplewick in 1785, and steam quickly displaced water in the Lancashire trade because a mill could then be built where the labour and the canal were.

Crompton's mule was scaled up and fitted with steam drive; Cartwright's power loom, patented in 1785, took another two decades to become practical. British raw cotton consumption rose more than tenfold in twenty years.

steps.name: The factory town and the first Factory Acts
steps.page:
By the 1830s the consequences were being counted: cholera in 1832, Chadwick's sanitary inquiry, and evidence to parliamentary commissions about children working twelve-hour days in mills and hauling in mines.

The Factory Act of 1833 limited children's hours in textile mills and, for the first time, appointed inspectors to enforce it. The Mines Act of 1842 followed. Neither went far, and both established that the state would regulate what went on inside a private factory.

name: Third Battle of Panipat
summary: Ahmad Shah Durrani's Afghan army defeated the Marathas at Panipat on 14 January 1761 in one of the largest battles of the eighteenth century.
body:
Part of [Maratha Empire](event:maratha-empire). Maratha expansion into the Punjab brought them against Ahmad Shah Durrani, ruler of Afghanistan, who had raided northern India repeatedly since 1748 and was supported by Rohilla and Awadh allies. The armies faced each other near Panipat for two months while the Afghans cut the Maratha supply lines.

The Marathas attacked on 14 January 1761. The centre held into the afternoon; when Vishwasrao, the peshwa's son, was killed, the line broke, and the Afghan reserve of camel-mounted swivel guns and cavalry completed the defeat. Casualties were very large and are not reliably known; estimates of Maratha dead on the day range widely, and many prisoners and camp followers were killed afterwards.

Ahmad Shah returned to Afghanistan and did not hold northern India. The Marathas recovered Delhi in 1771, but the losses among their leadership and the ten years of division that followed left the field to the [East India Company](event:english-east-india).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Battle_of_Panipat).

name: Rousseau's The Social Contract
summary: Jean-Jacques Rousseau's *The Social Contract* (1762) opens with the claim that man is born free and is everywhere in chains, and argues that a legitimate state is one in which citizens obey only laws they have made themselves, expressing a 'general will'.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Rousseau was a Genevan watchmaker's son who had reached his position in two earlier discourses: that the arts and sciences had corrupted morals rather than improved them, and that inequality originates in property and in the institutions built to protect it. He is the Enlightenment's great internal critic, and he quarrelled in turn with [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment), with Diderot and with Hume.

The contract in his account is not a bargain trading freedom for security, as in Hobbes, but the act by which a people constitutes itself as a people. Sovereignty then stays with the whole body of citizens and cannot be represented or delegated; a government is only its agent and may be dismissed. The general will is what citizens will as citizens, which is not the sum of what they severally want. The formula has been much disputed, since a ruler claiming to know the general will can claim to force people to be free, a phrase the text does use.

*Émile*, on education, appeared the same year; both books were condemned in Paris and Geneva and Rousseau spent years moving between refuges. His *Confessions* invented a kind of self-examination the Romantics took up wholesale. The Jacobins made him a patron of the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) and moved his remains to the Panthéon in 1794.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Social_Contract).

name: Mechanised spinning
summary: Between 1764 and 1779 three machines, Hargreaves's spinning jenny, Arkwright's water frame and Crompton's mule, broke the bottleneck in making yarn. Spinning moved out of the cottage and into the mill, and the factory system began with it.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). Under the old arrangement it took several hand spinners to keep one weaver supplied, and Kay's flying shuttle of 1733 had made the weaver faster still. James Hargreaves's jenny, built about 1764, let one worker turn eight spindles at once and eventually many more; its yarn was soft and could be used only as weft.

Richard Arkwright's water frame, patented in 1769, drew the fibre through rollers turning at different speeds and produced thread strong enough for warp, so that cloth could be made of cotton throughout. It was too large and too power-hungry for a house, so Arkwright built mills, at Cromford from 1771, water-driven and employing whole families on shifts around the clock. Samuel Crompton's mule of 1779 combined both principles and spun fine, strong yarn; steam-driven mules later carried over a thousand spindles each.

British cotton output rose enormously and cheap cloth was exported worldwide, undercutting Indian handloom weaving in India itself. The demand for raw cotton was met by slave plantations in the American south. Hargreaves's neighbours are said to have broken into his house and smashed his machines.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinning_jenny).

name: Voyages of James Cook
summary: Three Pacific voyages between 1768 and 1780 under James Cook, which charted New Zealand and the east coast of Australia, crossed the Antarctic Circle and mapped much of the Pacific.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). James Cook, a Yorkshire farm labourer's son who had learned surveying in the navy, commanded three voyages to the Pacific for the Admiralty and the Royal Society.

The first, in the Endeavour from 1768 to 1771, carried astronomers to Tahiti to observe the transit of Venus, then opened sealed orders to search for the supposed southern continent. Cook charted the two islands of New Zealand and the east coast of Australia, where he landed at Botany Bay in April 1770 and claimed the coast for Britain, and ran the ship onto the Great Barrier Reef.

The second, from 1772 to 1775, crossed the Antarctic Circle three times and circled the southern ocean at high latitude, establishing that no habitable southern continent existed. Cook used citrus, sauerkraut and fresh provisions against scurvy and lost few men to it, and carried a copy of Harrison's marine chronometer, which fixed longitude at sea.

The third, from 1776, searched for a northwest passage from the Pacific side, reached the Bering Strait and was stopped by ice. Cook was killed at Kealakekua Bay in Hawaii on 14 February 1779 in a fight over a stolen boat. The charts he produced were in use for a century, and the voyages preceded British settlement in Australia and the whaling and trading traffic that followed across the Pacific.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_James_Cook).

name: Napoleon Bonaparte
summary: French general who made himself emperor, dominated Europe for a decade, and left behind a legal code still in use across much of the world.
body:
Born on Corsica a year after France annexed it, Napoleon was trained at French military schools and made his name in the artillery during [the Revolution](item:french-revolution). Command in Italy and an expedition to Egypt built his reputation; in 1799 he [seized power](item:napoleon-coup) in a coup, and in 1804 crowned himself emperor.

As a commander he moved armies faster than his opponents could react and concentrated force at the decisive point; [Austerlitz](item:austerlitz) in 1805 is the usual textbook example. [The wars](item:napoleonic-wars) that carry his name put most of Europe under French control or influence, but Britain held the sea after [Trafalgar](item:trafalgar), Spain became an unwinnable guerrilla war, and [the invasion of Russia](item:russia-1812) in 1812 destroyed the Grande Armée. He abdicated in 1814, returned for a hundred days, and was beaten at [Waterloo](item:waterloo).

He died in British custody on Saint Helena. The Napoleonic Code, a centralised administration, the metric system and conscription outlasted him, and the nationalism his campaigns provoked ran through European politics for a century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon).

name: First Partition of Poland
summary: Russia, Prussia and Austria annexed about a third of the territory of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth by a treaty signed on 5 August 1772.
body:
The Commonwealth had an elective monarchy, a parliament in which a single deputy could veto legislation, and no standing army of any size, and by the middle of the eighteenth century it was effectively a Russian protectorate. A confederation formed at Bar in 1768 against Russian influence was suppressed after four years of fighting.

Frederick II of Prussia proposed a partition as a way of ending the crisis without a war between the three powers. The treaty was signed in St Petersburg on 5 August 1772: Russia took the lands east of the Dvina and the Dnieper, Prussia took Royal Prussia except Danzig and Thorn, and Austria took Galicia. Between them they took about 30 per cent of the territory and 4 million people.

The Polish parliament was assembled under military pressure and ratified it in 1773. It then founded the Commission of National Education, the first ministry of education in Europe, and the constitution of 3 May 1791 followed. Two further partitions, in 1793 and 1795, removed the state from the map until 1918.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Partition_of_Poland).

name: Pugachev's Rebellion
summary: A revolt of Cossacks, peasants and Volga peoples led by Yemelyan Pugachev, who claimed to be Peter III. It was the largest peasant rising in Russian history and was crushed in 1775.
body:
Yemelyan Pugachev, a Don Cossack deserter, declared himself the emperor Peter III, who had been deposed and killed in 1762, and raised the Yaik Cossacks in September 1773. The rising spread through the Ural mining districts and the middle Volga, drawing in serfs, Old Believers, Bashkirs, Tatars and factory workers.

Pugachev issued manifestos abolishing serfdom, taxes and conscription and granting land and the old faith. He besieged Orenburg through the winter of 1773, took Kazan in July 1774 and burned it. Landowners and officials were killed across a wide area, and the reprisals that followed were on the same scale.

Catherine II had to end the war with the Ottomans in 1774 to release troops. Pugachev was defeated near Tsaritsyn in August, handed over by his own officers, and executed in Moscow in January 1775. The government reorganised provincial administration in 1775 and tightened landlords' powers over serfs.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pugachev%27s_Rebellion).

name: Goethe's literary influence
summary: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was the dominant figure in German literature for half a century, as poet, dramatist, novelist, critic, court official and amateur scientist. *The Sorrows of Young Werther* made him famous across Europe in 1774, when he was twenty-four.
body:
*Werther* is a short novel in letters about a young man who kills himself over an unattainable love. It was a sensation: readers dressed in the hero's blue coat and yellow waistcoat, and it was blamed then and afterwards for a wave of imitative suicides. It belonged to *Sturm und Drang*, the movement that set feeling and individual genius against the rules of French classicism.

The Duke of Weimar brought him to court in 1775, and Goethe spent the rest of his life there, running mines, roads and the theatre and sitting on the privy council. A journey to Italy in 1786–88 turned him towards classical restraint. *Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship* (1795–96) established the German novel of formation, the *Bildungsroman*, and his lyrics and ballads were set to music by Schubert, Schumann and Wolf. His friendship and correspondence with Schiller shaped both men's work in the 1790s.

*Faust*, begun in his twenties and completed the year before his death in 1832, is the work he is measured by: a scholar's bargain with Mephistopheles that opens in a study and ends, in the second part, as a symbolic drama of the whole modern world. He also wrote on plant morphology and a theory of colour intended to refute [Newton](event:newton), which physicists rejected and painters read with interest.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Wolfgang_von_Goethe).

name: American Revolution
summary: Thirteen British colonies in North America went to war with Britain in 1775, declared independence in 1776 and won recognition of it in 1783. The new United States then wrote a federal constitution, and was the first modern republic founded on a written statement of natural rights.
body:
The quarrel followed the [Seven Years' War](event:seven-years-war), when Parliament tried to make the colonies pay a share of imperial defence through the Stamp Act, the Townshend duties and the tea tax. Colonists objected that they were being taxed by a body in which they were not represented, and that their own assemblies had long held that power. Boycotts, riots and Britain's coercive response to the destruction of tea in Boston harbour in 1773 hardened both sides, and shooting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775.

Britain's problem was distance and the absence of a decisive target. Washington's Continental Army had to be kept in being rather than made to win, and it survived Long Island, the loss of New York and Philadelphia and the winter at Valley Forge. Saratoga in 1777 brought France into the war in 1778, followed by Spain and the Dutch Republic, turning a colonial rebellion into a global one that stretched British forces from Gibraltar to India. A French fleet closed the Chesapeake and made [Yorktown](event:yorktown) a surrender rather than a siege that could be relieved.

Perhaps a fifth of the population stayed loyal to the Crown, and some 60,000 left, most for Canada. Native nations, most of which had sided with Britain as the power more likely to restrain settlement, lost their protector in the peace. Slavery survived the language of the [Declaration](event:declaration-independence): northern states began abolishing it, southern states did not, and the question was deferred into the [Constitution](event:us-constitution) and eventually into a civil war. The revolution's example, and the debt France ran up paying for it, contributed to the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) six years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution).

steps.name: Lexington and Concord
steps.page:
British regulars marched out of Boston on the night of 18 April 1775 to seize militia stores at Concord. Riders including Paul Revere raised the countryside ahead of them.

Shots were exchanged on Lexington green at dawn and again at Concord bridge, and the column was fired on from behind walls all the way back to Boston, losing some 270 men. Within weeks a militia army had besieged the city.

steps.name: Saratoga and the French alliance
steps.page:
A British army under Burgoyne moving south from Canada was fought to a standstill at Freeman's Farm and Bemis Heights and surrendered nearly 6,000 men at Saratoga on 17 October 1777.

It was the first surrender of a British army in the war, and it convinced France that the Americans could win. The treaties of alliance and commerce were signed in Paris on 6 February 1778, turning a colonial rebellion into a European war.

steps.name: The war moves south
steps.page:
Unable to force a decision in the north, Britain turned to the southern colonies, expecting loyalist support. Savannah fell in December 1778 and Charleston in May 1780, with the capture of a whole American army.

What followed was a partisan war of raids and reprisals. Greene's campaign traded ground for time, and Cornwallis, having won at Guilford Court House in March 1781 at ruinous cost, marched into Virginia with an army worn thin.

steps.name: The Treaty of Paris
steps.page:
Negotiations opened in Paris in 1782, with Franklin, Adams and Jay dealing separately with Britain despite the French alliance and getting better terms for it.

The treaty signed on 3 September 1783 recognised the United States as independent and granted a western boundary at the Mississippi, more than the fighting had won, over the heads of the Native nations who had fought as British allies. Britain settled separately with France and Spain the same day.

name: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations
summary: Adam Smith's *An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations*, published in 1776, argued that a nation's wealth is the goods its people produce rather than the bullion it holds, and that specialisation and voluntary exchange increase it. It founded economics as a subject.
body:
Part of [The Enlightenment](event:enlightenment). Smith was professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow and had already published *The Theory of Moral Sentiments*, which grounds morality in sympathy. The two books are usually read together, since the later one assumes the earlier one's account of what moves people.

The famous opening describes a pin factory: ten workers who each perform one operation make far more pins than ten working separately, and the extent of that division of labour is limited by the size of the market, which is the case for wide trade. Prices in a competitive market carry information and draw resources where they are wanted; the butcher and the brewer supply dinner from their own interest rather than from benevolence, and are led "as by an invisible hand" to an outcome none of them intended. The phrase occurs once in the book.

Its polemical target was mercantilism: tariffs, chartered monopolies, colonial trade restrictions, and the habit of treating exports as gain and imports as loss. Smith was no apologist for merchants, who in his account seldom meet together without conspiring against the public, and he argued for public works, schooling and taxes falling more than proportionately on the rich. Its arguments shaped nineteenth-century free trade policy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wealth_of_Nations).

name: Watt's steam engine
summary: James Watt patented a steam engine with a separate condenser in 1769 and, in partnership with Matthew Boulton, began selling engines in 1776. It burned a fraction of the fuel of earlier designs, and once adapted to turn a shaft it could drive machinery anywhere.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine, working since 1712, condensed steam inside the cylinder to make a vacuum, which meant cooling and reheating the whole cylinder on every stroke. It was useful only where fuel was nearly free, at the pithead. Watt, repairing a model of one at Glasgow, saw that condensing in a separate vessel would let the cylinder stay hot; his engines cut coal consumption by roughly three quarters.

Turning that into a business took Boulton's capital and John Wilkinson's cannon-boring machine, which could bore a cylinder round enough for a piston to seal against. Watt added double action, the sun-and-planet gear to produce rotary motion, a centrifugal governor to hold the speed steady, and the parallel motion linkage he was proudest of. Boulton and Watt charged royalties calculated on the fuel their engines saved, and defended the patent aggressively; its extension to 1800 is often said to have delayed rival designs, particularly high-pressure engines.

Rotary steam power freed factories from rivers, drained deeper mines, and drove the mills, forges, locomotives and ships of the following century. The SI unit of power is named after him, and horsepower was his own marketing comparison against a mill horse.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watt_steam_engine).

name: Declaration of Independence
summary: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776, announcing that the thirteen colonies were free and independent states. Its second paragraph, asserting that all men are created equal and hold unalienable rights, became the most quoted statement of the American founding.
body:
Part of [American Revolution](event:american-revolution). Congress voted for independence on 2 July, on a resolution moved by Richard Henry Lee, and approved the wording two days later. Thomas Jefferson wrote the draft in about two weeks; Franklin and Adams suggested changes, and Congress cut roughly a quarter of it, including a passage blaming George III for the slave trade that delegates from South Carolina and Georgia would not accept.

Most of the text is a list of grievances against the king, framed to show a deliberate design to establish tyranny. That was necessary rather than rhetorical: the argument was that the colonies were entitled to dissolve their allegiance, and eighteenth-century readers expected such a case to be made in legal form. The philosophical preamble drew on Locke and on the Virginia Declaration of Rights written weeks earlier by George Mason.

Its claim of equality stood beside the enslavement of about a fifth of the population, and Jefferson himself held people in bondage. Abolitionists, Lincoln at Gettysburg, the Seneca Falls convention of 1848 and the civil rights movement all appealed to the same sentence, which is why it has been called a promissory note. The document was also a diplomatic instrument: independent states could make treaties, and the alliance with France followed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence).

name: Tay Son Rebellion in Vietnam
summary: The Tay Son brothers led a rebellion from the Vietnamese highlands that overthrew both ruling families, repelled Siamese and Qing invasions, and briefly united the country. The movement fractured after 1792 and was defeated in 1802 by Nguyen Anh, who founded the Nguyen dynasty.
body:
Vietnam had been divided for two centuries between the Trinh lords in the north and the Nguyen in the south, both governing in the name of a powerless Le emperor. Three brothers from the village of Tay Son rose in 1771 against Nguyen taxation, took the southern capital, and by 1786 had destroyed both houses. They redistributed confiscated land, cancelled debts, and recruited officials on ability rather than birth.

Nguyen Hue, the ablest brother, destroyed a Siamese fleet and army at Rach Gam–Xoai Mut in 1785, and in the first days of 1789 marched north and routed a large Qing army at Ngoc Hoi–Dong Da during the lunar new year, the victory best remembered in Vietnam. He took the throne as the Quang Trung emperor and began reforms of the currency, the land registers and the examinations, promoting the vernacular *nom* script in place of classical Chinese.

He died in 1792 at about forty, and the movement split among his heirs. Nguyen Anh, a survivor of the destroyed southern house, rebuilt his forces in the far south with French advisers and arms obtained through the missionary Pigneau de Béhaine, and took Hue and Hanoi in 1802. As the Gia Long emperor he ruled a unified country under the name Vietnam.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tây_Sơn_dynasty).

name: Siege of Yorktown
summary: A combined American and French army trapped Lord Cornwallis's British force on the Virginia peninsula at Yorktown while a French fleet held off relief by sea. Cornwallis surrendered about 7,000 men on 19 October 1781, effectively ending the fighting in America.
body:
Part of [American Revolution](event:american-revolution). Cornwallis had marched north from the Carolinas, where a campaign of small actions had worn his army down, and was ordered to fortify a deep-water port. Washington had been planning to attack New York; on learning that Admiral de Grasse was bringing the French West Indies fleet to the Chesapeake, he marched his own army and Rochambeau's some 700 kilometres south, leaving campfires burning to disguise the move.

The decisive engagement was naval. De Grasse fought off the British relief fleet at the Battle of the Chesapeake on 5 September, after which Cornwallis could be neither reinforced nor taken off. The siege opened on 28 September; French engineers dug the approach trenches, and on 14 October assaults carried redoubts 9 and 10, one of them led by Alexander Hamilton, which let the second parallel reach the river. With his works collapsing under bombardment and a night crossing broken up by a storm, Cornwallis asked for terms.

The garrison marched out to lay down its arms, Cornwallis pleading illness and sending a deputy. News of the surrender brought down Lord North's government in London in March 1782 and opened the negotiations that produced the Treaty of Paris in 1783. Fighting went on elsewhere, in the West Indies, at Gibraltar and in India, but not in the thirteen states.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Yorktown).

name: Chakri Dynasty founded in Siam
summary: General Chao Phraya Chakri took the Siamese throne in 1782 as Rama I, founded the dynasty that still reigns in Thailand, and moved the capital across the river to Bangkok.
body:
The old Siamese capital of Ayutthaya had been destroyed by a Burmese army in 1767. King Taksin drove the Burmese out and rebuilt the kingdom over the following fifteen years from a new capital at Thonburi; in 1782, amid a revolt and reports that the king had become unstable, Taksin was deposed and executed, and his leading general was invited to take the throne.

Rama I moved the seat of government to the east bank at Bangkok and built a walled royal city with the Grand Palace and the temple of the Emerald Buddha, deliberately modelled on the lost Ayutthaya. He had the law recodified in the Three Seals Code, convened a council to revise the Buddhist canon, and rebuilt the administration and army, which held off further Burmese invasions.

His successors met European expansion by conceding what they had to and reforming quickly: Mongkut and Chulalongkorn opened trade, abolished slavery by stages, built railways and telegraphs and centralised the provinces, ceding border territories to Britain and France to keep the core. Siam was the only state in Southeast Asia never colonised. Absolute monarchy ended in a coup in 1932, and the dynasty has continued through wars, constitutions and repeated coups since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chakri_Dynasty).

name: United States Constitution
summary: Delegates meeting at Philadelphia in the summer of 1787 wrote a constitution replacing the Articles of Confederation with a federal government of three branches. Ratified in 1788 and in force from 1789, it is the oldest written national constitution still operating.
body:
Part of [American Revolution](event:american-revolution). The confederation could not levy taxes or regulate trade, and Shays's Rebellion in Massachusetts in 1786–87 persuaded many that it could not keep order either. The convention was called to amend it and wrote a new instrument instead, sitting behind closed doors through a hot summer with Washington presiding and James Madison taking the notes that are the main record of what was said.

The design was a set of compromises. Large and small states were reconciled by a House apportioned by population and a Senate with two seats each. Slavery was accommodated: enslaved people counted as three-fifths of a person for representation, the slave trade was protected from prohibition until 1808, and escapees had to be returned. None of it is named in the text, which avoids the word. Powers were separated and set against one another along lines drawn from [Montesquieu](event:montesquieu-spirit), with an executive chosen by an electoral college rather than by Congress or by voters directly.

Ratification was contested state by state and was argued out in the *Federalist Papers*; several states ratified on the understanding that a bill of rights would follow, and the first ten amendments were adopted in 1791.
